To assess whether there is an interplay between AtDAO1 and AtGH3s, we analyzed AtDAO1 transcript levels in gh3.3, gh3.5, and gh3.6 single and triple mutant stamens at stages 10-11 (pooled together). As shown in Figure 3C, AtDAO1 transcript was slightly but significantly decreased in gh3.3, whereas it was increased in gh3.5 and gh3.6 single mutant stamens. Similar to gh3.3, AtDAO1 expression was significantly downregulated in gh3.3, gh3.5, gh3.6 triple mutant stamens (Figure 3D). In addition, we analyzed the expression of AtGH3s in dao1 mutant stamens. Both AtGH3.3 and AtGH3.6 were significantly upregulated in dao1-1 and dao1-3, while AtGH3.5 was unchanged in dao1-1 and significantly upregulated in dao1-3 (Figure 3E-G). Both dao1-1 and dao1-3 mutant lines contain a T-DNA insertion located in the first exon and in the promoter, respectively. AtDAO1 transcripts are not detected in dao1-1 and are reduced to 10% of the wild type in dao1-3 (Zhang et al. ), which could account for the differences observed in AtGH3.5 expression.

To determine whether AtDAO1 is expressed at the same stages as AtGH3s and whether it is regulated by ARF8, we analyzed AtDAO1 transcript levels in Col-0 and arf8-7 stamens at stages from 9 to 12 of flower development. As shown in Figure 3H, AtDAO1 expression in Col-0 is low at stages 9 and 10, increases at stage 11, when JA concentration peaks, and decreases at stage 12. This result is in contrast with AtGH3.3 and AtGH3.5 expression, which is mainly observed at stage 10, while is comparable to AtGH3.6 expression, which increases at both stages 10 and 11 of flower development. Interestingly, in arf8-7 mutant stamens compared to Col-0, AtDAO1 expression significantly increases at stages 9 and 10, and decreases at stages 11 and 12 (Figure 3H), while that of AtGH3s is mainly downregulated from stage 9 to 12.

These results show that AtDAO1 is predominantly expressed at later stages than AtGH3s and strongly suggest that both are regulated by AtARF8, while a compensatory expression of AtGH3s and AtDAO1 occurs in gh3s and dao1 mutants, likely modulating free IAA levels during stamen elongation.
Mutations in  GH3  Genes Affect Free IAA Levels in Arabidopsis Flower Buds

Both auxin and JA have a promotive effect on stamen elongation; therefore, GH3s could affect stamen development by interfering with endogenous levels of free IAA or JA, as in adventitious roots formation (Cardarelli and Cecchetti ; Gutierrez et al. ; Nagpal et al. ). To discern between these two possibilities, free IAA levels, IAA-Asp content and JA levels, were evaluated in Col-0 and gh3.3 gh3.5 gh3.6 triple mutant flower buds at stages 10-12 (pooled together), in which IAA and JA content is detectable (Cecchetti et al. ; Nagpal et al. ).

As shown in Figure 4A, IAA levels were significantly higher in gh3.3, gh3.5, and gh3.6 triple mutant flower buds (about 2-fold), while the IAA-Asp amount showed a significant decrease (Figure 4B). In contrast, free JA levels slightly increased in the triple mutant flower buds, although no significant differences were observed compared to Col-0 (Figure 4C).

Group II SlGH3s  Genes and  SlDAO2  Are Expressed in Tomato Stamens During Development

Phylogenetic analysis showed that AtGH3.3, AtGH3.5, and AtGH3.6 cluster in the same phylogenetic group II of SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3, SlGH3.4, SlGH3.9, and SlGH3.15. Among SlGH3s, SlGH3.9 and SlGH3.15 belong to the same subgroup as AtGH3.5 and AtGH3.6, whereas SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3, and SlGH3.4 belong to the same subgroup as AtGH3.3 (Figure S2), as previously demonstrated (Kumar et al. ; Liao et al. ). By using AtGH3.3, AtGH3.5, and AtGH3.6 proteins as query sequences for blastp with Sol Genomics Network, we analyzed the degree of similarity between Arabidopsis and tomato sequences (Table S3). We found that all three SlGH3.2, SlGH3.4, and SlGH3.3 are highly homologous to AtGH3.3 (78.22%, 75.78%, and 75.67%, respectively), while SlGH3.9 and SlGH3.15 are highly homologous to both AtGH3.5 and AtGH3.6 (81.7% and 83.01%, respectively, and 81.35 and 79.87, respectively).

To assess a possible involvement of these genes during stamen development in tomato, we analyzed their expression in stamens from stage 0 to stage 4, roughly corresponding to flower developmental stages 9-13 in Arabidopsis (Table S5; Brukhin et al. ; Cecchetti et al. ; Khaliluev et al. ; Marzi et al. ; Mazzucato et al. ; Smyth et al. ). As shown in Figure 5A, in wild type (Chico III) stamens, SlGH3.2 was almost undetectable at stage 0, significantly increased from stage 1 to stage 2, while it decreased at stages 3 and 4. Similarly, the expression of SlGH3.3 was almost undetectable at stage 0, increased at stages 1-2, and decreased at stages 3-4 (Figure 5B). The expression of SlGH3.4 was almost undetectable at stages 0 and 1, increased from stage 2 to stage 3, and decreased at stage 4 (Figure 5C). The expression of SlGH3.9 was low at stage 0, increased at stages 1-2, and decreased at stages 3 and 4 (Figure 5D), while that of SlGH3.15 was barely detectable at stages 0-1 and significantly increased from stage 2 to stage 4 (Figure 5E).

Similarly, SlDAO2 phylogenetic analysis showed a high homology to AtDAO1 (59%; Table S3); thus, we evaluated its expression in stamens at stages from 0 to 4 of flower development. As shown in Figure 5F, in wild type stamens, SlDAO2 expression peaks at stage 2 and significantly decreases at stages 3 and 4 of flower development.

These results show that all SlGH3s and SlDAO2 are expressed during stamen development in tomato. SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3 and SlGH3.9 act predominantly at early stages (stages 1 and 2 corresponding to stages 10 and 11 in Arabidopsis), SlGH3.4 and SlGH3.15 at late stages (3 and 4 corresponding to stages 12 and 13 in Arabidopsis), while SlDAO2 mainly is expressed at stage 0-2, corresponding to stage 9 and 11 in Arabidopsis.
SlARF8A  and  SlARF8B  Expression Is Reduced in the Tomato Parthenocarpic pat Mutant

The tomato parthenocarpic pat mutant shows an impaired stamen development, which affects plant fertility (Mazzucato et al. ). In agreement, we found that at the beginning of stage 3, when flower disclosure occurs, pat mutants developed significantly shorter stamens than the wild type (Chico III) (Figure 6A,B), similarly to arf8-7 mutants in Arabidopsis. Thus, we analyzed the expression of the two AtARF8 homologs in tomato, namely SlARF8A and SlARF8B (Liu et al. ; Zouine et al. ), which show a high homology to the Arabidopsis gene (67% each, Table S3). As shown in Figure 6C,D, we found that in pat mutant stamens compared to wild type, SlARF8A transcript level is unchanged at stage 0 and significantly lower at stage 1, while SlARF8B expression is downregulated at both stages compared to Chico III (Figure 6C,D).

SlGH3s  Genes and  SlDAO1  Expression Is Deregulated in the Tomato Parthenocarpic pat Mutant

According to the previous section, we speculated that SlGH3s and SlDAO2 genes could be involved in the regulation of stamen growth in tomato, similarly to Arabidopsis. To verify this hypothesis, we compared the expression of group II SlGH3s genes in Chico III and pat stamens at stages 0, 1 and 2 of flower development, corresponding to stages 9-11 in Arabidopsis. As shown in Figure 7, the expression of SlGH3.2 and SlGH3.3 was significantly increased at stages 0 and 1 in pat mutant stamens compared to Chico III, while it increased and decreased significantly, respectively, at stage 2 (Figure 7A,B). The expression of SlGH3.4 in pat stamens was decreased at stage 0, slightly increased at stage 1 and decreased again at stage 2, compared to Chico III (Figure 7C). The expression of SlGH3.9 in pat stamens was upregulated at stages 0 and 2, and downregulated at stage 1 (Figure 7D), while that of SlGH3.15 was upregulated at stage 1 and repressed at stage 2 compared to Chico III (Figure 7E). In addition, we analyzed the expression of SlDAO2 in pat mutant stamens at stages 0-2 of flower development and we found that it remained unchanged at stages 0 and 1, while it significantly decreased at stage 2, compared to Chico III (Figure 7F).

These results indicate that all SlGH3s genes are deregulated in pat stamens, most of them being upregulated at stages 0 and 1, while SlDAO2 is downregulated only at stage 2, suggesting that the conjugation activity of SlGH3, on IAA or JA, might be increased, while DAO2-dependent IAA oxidizing activity is decreased in pat stamens.
Tomato pat Mutants Have a Decreased Auxin Content in Flower Buds

To evaluate whether SlGH3 and SlDAO1 gene deregulation affects hormone content in the pat mutants, we compared the amount of free endogenous IAA, IAA-Asp, and JA levels in Chico III and pat stamens at stages 1-2 (pooled together), as auxin and JA are highly detectable in pre-anthesis stages in tomato (Gillaspy et al. ; Khaliluev et al. ). As shown in Figure 8, IAA levels significantly decreased in pat stamens compared to Chico III ones (Figure 8A), while IAA-Asp abundance was significantly increased (Figure 8B). Interestingly, in contrast to Arabidopsis, JA content was significantly increased in pat mutant stamens compared to the control (Figure 8C). These results indicate that in tomato, similarly to Arabidopsis, SlGH3s and SlDAO1 play a central role during stamen maturation, regulating not only auxin homeostasis but also JA levels to achieve appropriate organ development.

Discussion

Late stamen development is regulated by auxin through changes in auxin concentration and localization, during subsequent developmental stages (Cardarelli and Cecchetti ). The biosynthesis and distribution of auxin in different stamen tissues have been extensively studied (Cardarelli and Cecchetti ; Cecchetti et al. ). However, the role of the main auxin inactivation pathways, which include conjugation to amino acids by GH3s and oxidation by DAO1, remains elusive.

In this study, we show through qRT-PCR analysis that AtGH3.3, AtGH3.5, and AtGH3.6 are downregulated, whereas AtDAO1 is upregulated in arf8-7 stamens during late flower development (Figures 1, 2, 3), indicating the involvement of these genes in ARF8-controlled stamen filament elongation. These data are consistent with previous reports on the role of ARF8 in auxin signaling in reproductive organs (Ghelli et al. ; Nagpal et al. ). By analyzing the expression of AtGH3.3, AtGH3.5, and AtGH3.6 in Col-0 stamens, the phenotype of the gh3.3 gh3.5 gh3.6 triple mutants flowers, as well as free and conjugated IAA levels in flower buds, we demonstrated that GH3s modulate free auxin levels mainly during early stages of late flower development (stages 10 and 11) by catalyzing its conjugation to amino acids. Indeed, the auxin-inducible genes AtGH3s are expressed in Col-0 stamens with partially overlapping expression profiles, and their transcript levels are detected mainly at stage 10 when auxin concentration is high, and at stage 11 when it starts to decrease (Hayashi et al. ). Among GH3s, AtGH3.3 and AtGH3.5 were the most expressed during stamen development, while AtGH3.6 was expressed at lower levels (Figure 1). Consistently, the significant increase in free IAA and the concomitant decrease in IAA-Asp in gh3.3 gh3.5 gh3.6 triple mutant flower buds provide direct evidence that AtGH3s catalyze auxin conjugation during late development (Figure 4). In agreement with the observed increase in free IAA and the promotive role of auxin on filament elongation, the gh3.3 gh3.5 gh3.6 triple mutant flowers exhibit stamens that are 24.8% longer than Col-0 stamens at stage 14. Our results confirm previous studies that demonstrated the role of AtGH3s in catalyzing IAA conjugation to amino acids and in particular in IAA-Asp formation (Ludwig-Muller ; Staswick et al. ). Furthermore, by measuring the content of free JA, which is found to be unchanged in gh3.3 gh3.5 gh3 triple mutants versus Col-0 flower buds, we ruled out the possibility that the AtGH3s genes act on the formation of JA conjugates during early stages of stamen late development, as observed for adventitious root formation (Gutierrez et al. ).

We also found that auxin levels in stamens require a fine-tuned balance between both conjugation and degradation via AtGH3s and via AtDAO1, respectively. This is achieved by the compensatory gene expression induced by mutations in individual AtGH3s genes that activate or inhibit the transcription of the other AtGH3s, as well as that of AtDAO1. Indeed, altered expression of other AtGH3s and AtDAO1 is observed in all single mutants that have shorter stamens than Col-0. On the other hand, the upregulation of AtGH3.3, AtGH3.5, and AtGH3.6 in dao1 mutants (Figure 3) suggests a feedback loop in which decreased auxin degradation triggers increased conjugation by GH3s, possibly as a compensatory response to restore auxin homeostasis. However, the absence of all three AtGH3s in the gh3s triple mutant promotes stamen elongation and triggers the downregulation of AtDAO1, consistent with AtDAO1 acting downstream of AtGH3s by oxidizing the IAA-Asp and IAA-Glu conjugates produced by AtGH3s (Hayashi et al. ). Consistently, AtDAO1 expression in stamens was mainly observed at stage 11, whereas AtGH3s are mainly expressed at stage 10, corresponding to auxin concentration maxima in stamens (Cecchetti et al. ). Furthermore, since auxin negatively regulates JA biosynthesis by acting on both JA biosynthetic genes, AtDAD1 and AtOPR3, JA levels at stage 11 increase in Arabidopsis wild type stamens (Cecchetti et al. ). This suggests that JA may induce AtDAO1 expression in stamens, as previously shown during adventitious root formation (Lakehal, Dob, et al. ).

We also show that dao1-1 and dao1-3 stamens are 21% and 16.2% shorter than Col-0 stamens, respectively, likely due to the upregulation of AtGH3s in dao1 mutants (Figure 3), as GH3s have been shown to respond rapidly to environmental factors that increase cellular IAA levels (Zhang et al. ).

To assess whether the ARF8-GH3s-DAO1 module is conserved during tomato stamen development, we identified five SlGH3s members belonging to group II as well as SlDAO2, which is homologous to AtDAO1. We found that SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3, and SlGH3.4 have the highest percentage of protein identity to AtGH3.3, and SlGH3.9 and SlGH3.15 the highest percentage of protein identity with AtGH3.5 and AtGH3.6 (Figure S2; Table S3). Similar to Arabidopsis, by analyzing the expression of five SlGH3 members in Chico III tomato stamens and in the pat mutant, which is defective in stamen growth, free and conjugated auxin, and JA content in stamens, we show that the SlGH3 genes are involved in auxin conjugation during stamen development also in tomato. Indeed, all these genes are expressed in Chico III stamens with partially overlapping profiles, as SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3, and SlGH3.9 transcript levels are mainly high at stages 1 and 2, roughly corresponding to Arabidopsis stages 10 and 11, while SlGH3.15 and SlGH3.4 are mainly expressed later at stages 3 and 4 (Figure 5). In agreement with the reduced stamen elongation phenotype, pat mutant stamens show reduced free IAA, increased IAA-Asp, and an increased expression at stage 0 of SlGH3.2, SlGH3.3, and SlGH3.9, while SlGH3.4 and SlGH3.15 are upregulated at stage 1. Our data also suggest a role for ARF8 in proper stamen development in tomato. Indeed, the AtARF8 orthologs SlARF8A and SlARF8B are expressed in Chico III stamens at stages 0 and 1, whereas they are downregulated in pat stamens (Figure 6), consistent with the impaired auxin homeostasis and reduced stamen elongation observed in these mutants (Liu et al. ; Zouine et al. ). The loss of SlARF8 in tomato is consistent with the role of AtARF8 in Arabidopsis, where it is known to regulate stamen filament elongation (Ghelli et al. ; Nagpal et al. ; Tabata et al. ). These data are also consistent with recent findings showing that pat is characterized by a mutation in the HD-ZIP gene SlHB15A, which has a pleiotropic phenotype and affects auxin signaling, deregulating the expression of several auxin-related genes such as SlARF8, SlARF9, SlIAA9, and SlIAA14 (Clepet et al. ; Picarella et al. ; Ruiu et al. ). A direct interaction between pat and SlARF7 has been demonstrated (Clepet et al. ), and the downregulation of SlARF8 at early stages in the pat ovary has been also shown (Ruiu et al. ). Therefore, it is likely that pat acts upstream of both SlARF transcription factors to control auxin-inactivating enzymes.

However, in contrast to Arabidopsis, the reduced stamen length and other developmental defects observed in the pat mutants are likely a consequence of disrupted auxin as well as of JA homeostasis. Furthermore, auxin and JA have antagonistic effects during the abscission process that occurs in tomato flowers (Liu, Cheng, et al. ). The increase in JA content correlates with the misregulation of SlGH3 and SlDAO2 in pat tomato stamens. This is consistent with the different role of JA in stamen development in Arabidopsis and tomato, which is probably due to the primary role of this hormone in ovary development in tomato. Indeed, the Arabidopsis coi1 mutant, defective in JA perception, shows reduced stamen elongation and anther dehiscence, as well as non-functional pollen, whereas the tomato jasmonic-acid insensitive1 (jai1) mutant which is defective in the ortholog of Arabidopsis COI1, shows reduced pollen viability and female sterility, without any defect in anther dehiscence (Niwa et al. ). However, in tomato flower buds, auxin accumulation starts from stages 0 and 1 (Goldental-Cohen et al. ; Mazzucato et al. ), while JA is detectable from stage 2 (Niwa et al. ), suggesting that downregulation of SlGH3.4, which occurs at stages 1 and 2 in pat mutant stamens reduces JA conjugation, thus leading to an increase in free JA. Consistent with this, the role of AtGH3s in JA conjugation has already been demonstrated in Arabidopsis during adventitious root formation (Gutierrez et al. ). However, we cannot rule out the possibility that the elevated JA levels in tomato stamens are due to altered expression of SlGH3s other than those homologous to AtGH3s. Further work will be necessary to unveil the specific role of JA in relation to GH3s in tomato stamen development.
Conclusions

This study provides insights into the role of AtGH3s and AtDAO1 genes in stamen development, highlighting the compensatory regulation among these genes and their involvement in the regulation of auxin homeostasis. Our results reveal that AtGH3s regulate stamen elongation by conjugating auxin and thus reducing free IAA at the initial stages of late flower development, immediately after the auxin maximum. In contrast, AtDAO1 acts predominantly at the final stages of flower development. We also show that AtGH3s and AtDAO1 orthologs regulate auxin homeostasis in tomato stamens, highlighting the evolutionary conservation of these processes. The stable JA levels observed in Arabidopsis gh3s mutants stamens exclude a potential role for AtGH3s in JA conjugation in this plant species. In contrast, the elevated JA levels in the tomato pat mutant suggest that SlGH3s are involved in the regulation of JA homeostasis during tomato stamen development. These findings are consistent with the different roles of JA in male and female fertility across Arabidopsis and tomato species.

passages.text: Metabolomics analysis reveals dynamic changes of volatile and non-volatile metabolites during the scenting process of jasmine tea

To explore the dynamic changes in 'Round leaf' jasmine tea (RT) during the scenting process, targeted metabolomics and HS-SPME-GC-MS were used to identify the non-volatile and volatile compounds, and compare them with double-petal jasmine tea (DT). The analysis of taste activity values indicated that Asp, Thea, and Glu played significant roles in shaping the flavor profile of RT. The volatile compounds methyl anthranilate, benzyl acetate, linalool, indole, methyl benzoate and methyl salicylate were the key aroma compounds of jasmine tea. The volatiles (E)-3-hexenyl acetate, (E)-beta-ocimene and benzeneacetaldehyde significantly contributed to the elegance and freshness of RT. Additionally, the aroma compounds in RT reached saturation during the fourth scenting process (S4). Notably, RT reached better quality in S4 while DT reached better quality in S5. It can provide a scientific basis for the optimization of RT quality and its application in production.
Highlights
The key floral volatile compounds in jasmine tea were formed during the scenting process.
The six key aroma compounds of jasmine tea were identified.
The Asp, Thea and Glu non-volatile compounds contributed to the flavor of RT.
The three aroma compounds contributed significantly to the elegance and freshness of RT.
Introduction

Jasmine tea is a reprocessed tea, one of the representative historical tea of China, mainly produced in Fujian, Guangxi and Sichuan provinces. It is made from fresh jasmine flowers and green tea, in which the aroma of jasmine flowers is fully adsorbed by the base tea, also known as the scenting process. The special scenting process endows jasmine tea with a fresh and elegant floral aroma, and a mellow-brisk taste, making it popular among consumers. Jasmine flowers are prerequisite for processing jasmine tea, because the aroma quality of flowers significantly influences the final flavor of the product. Therefore, jasmine flower cultivars with high aroma quality are crucial for the development of the jasmine tea industry. However, the cultivars used in the current production are basically double-petal jasmine (Jasminum sambac cv. Bifoliatum), relatively simple cultivars, and have a single flavor, restricting the development of the jasmine industry. Therefore, there is an urgent need for jasmine varieties with high aroma quality and rich fragrance to provide fresh flower sources for jasmine tea processing.

The aroma plays a crucial role in determining the overall quality of jasmine tea. Previous research on jasmine tea mainly focused on the scenting techniques, scenting processes, and the use of different basic tea. The primary aroma compounds in jasmine tea were identified as benzyl acetate, methyl anthranilate, linalool and so forth using GC-MS. proposed the 'jasmine tea flavor' (JTF) index, indicating a positive correlation between the JTF index and the quality of jasmine tea. HS-SPME-GC-MS is a widely adopted method for identifying volatile organic compounds in tea owing to its convenience, fast analysis, and low cost.

Jasminum sambac cv. 'Round leaf' has a high propagation coefficient, high seedling rate, vigorous growth of surviving plants, and large flower yield. The development and application of jasmine tea with notable market potential is conducive to broadening the types of jasmine tea products. Currently, Jasminum sambac cv. 'Round leaf' is largely unutilized and has been used for scenting jasmine tea for the first time. We developed a new jasmine tea product using the 'Round leaf' jasmine variety and investigated its characteristic flavor compounds, as well as its differences from traditional double-petal jasmine tea during the scenting process. Therefore, we conducted targeted metabolomics and HS-SPME-GC-MS metabolomics analysis on two types of jasmine tea during the scenting process and one type of base tea. It provides a theoretical reference for developing innovative jasmine tea products and elucidating the aroma formation mechanisms of jasmine tea during the scenting process.
Materials and methods
Materials

All jasmine tea samples were made from green tea (Camellia sinensis 'Fuding Dahaocha', base tea, BT) and jasmine flowers (Jasminum sambac cv. 'Round leaf' and double-petal Jasminum sambac cv. Bifoliatum) that were cultivated in Fuzhou, China (26 08'18'' N, 119 24'05'' E). During the production of jasmine tea, the temperature and humidity for picking jasmine were 35 +- 2  C and 55 +- 5 %, respectively. Two types of jasmine tea products were obtained: 'Round leaf' jasmine tea (RT) and double-petal jasmine tea (DT).
Flowchart of jasmine tea scenting process (A) and sensory review (B).
Fig. 1

The scenting process of jasmine tea followed the Chinese national standard "Technique specification for processing of jasmine tea" (GB/T 34779-2017) The jasmine tea scenting process was carried out at Fuzhou Nanxian Tea Products Co., Ltd. from July to August 2022, as shown in Fig. 1A. The jasmine flower buds was picked on the sunny afternoon, then the flowers were maintained. When the flowers have bloomed to about 60 %, they were screened using a sifting tool. When the screened flowers have bloomed to about 80 % ~ 90 %, the base tea (BT) and flowers were blended to absorb the fragrance of the flowers. To ensure even fragrance absorption, the flower and tea mixture was periodically spread during scenting to release heat. The critical step regulated heat accumulation while maintaining appropriate environmental parameters: temperature at 40-45  C. When the scenting process was completed, the flowers was separated from the tea and then undergo a final drying phase to stabilize the absorbed fragrance. The scenting process was performed five times and named S1 (RT1, DT1), S2 (RT2, DT2), S3 (RT3, DT3), S4 (RT4, DT4), S5 (RT5, DT5). Three biological replicates were set up for each sample, and 33 samples were stored at -20  C in a refrigerator.
Sensory evaluation of jasmine tea

A professionally trained sensory panel (two females and three males) evaluated the quality attributes of jasmine tea samples. The sensory evaluation was conducted in accordance with the standard of the Methodology of Sensory Evaluation of Tea (GB/T 23776-2018) regulated by China. Briefly, 3 g of jasmine tea was brewed in 150 mL of boiling water for 3 min initially and for 5 min subsequently. The samples were graded using a composite score derived from five standardized parameters on a 100-point scale. Evaluations were conducted based on the appearance, aroma, liquor color, taste, and infused leaf of the samples, with descriptive comments provided for each sample. When describing sensory terms, the standard of Tea Vocabulary for Sensory Evaluation (GB/T 14487-2017) was used. National law does not require ethical approval for sensory assessments, so appropriate steps were taken to protect the privacy and rights of participants. Informed consent was obtained in writing from all study participants following a comprehensive briefing on experimental procedures. The research protocol strictly adhered to established ethical guidelines, ensuring full compliance with privacy preservation and participant rights throughout the investigation.
Determining free amino acids, catechins and purine alkaloids

According to the method reported by, the free amino acid content was determined using an aminoquinolyl-N-hydroxysuccinimidyl carbamate derived Ultra Performance Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) assay. We used the Nexera X2 LC-30A ultra-HPLC (UHPLC, Shimadzu, Japan), 4500 triple quadrupole MS (Sciex, USA) and FLM C18 reverse-phase column (2.6 mum, 2.1 x 100 mm) for analysis. The catechin composition was determined by HPLC with an FLM C18 reverse-phase column. Moreover, UPLC--MS/MS method was used to determine purine alkaloid content. The taste activity value (TAV) was calculated with reference to.
HS-SPME-GC-MS identification
HS-SPME extraction conditions

The sample was ground into a powder in liquid nitrogen. The 0.50 g powder was transferred immediately to a 20 mL head-space vial (Agilent, Palo Alto, CA, USA), containing 2 mL of NaCl saturated solution (China National Medicines Corporation Ltd., Beijing, China) and 10 muL of internal standard solution. The standards were prepared using n-hexane (>=99 %, Merck). The vials were sealed using crimp-top caps with TFE-silicone headspace septa (Agilent). At the time of SPME analysis, each vial was placed in 60  C for 5 min, then a 120 mum DVB/CWR/PDMS fibre (Agilent) was exposed to the headspace of the sample for 15 min at 60  C.
GC-MS detection

The volatile compounds (VOCs) were identified and quantified via an Agilent Model 7890B GC and a 7000D mass spectrometer (Agilent, Folsom, CA, USA) with a 30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 mum DB-5MS (5 % phenyl-polymethylsiloxane) capillary column (Agilent J&W Scientific, Folsom, CA, USA). The carrier gas was high-purity helium (99.999 %). The injector temperature was maintained at 250  C and the detector at 280  C. The oven temperature was programmed from 40  C (3.5 min), increasing to 100  C at 10  C/min, to 180  C at 7  C/min, and to 280  C at 25  C/min, hold for 5 min.

Mass spectra were recorded in electron impact (EI) ionization mode at 70 eV with the quadrupole mass detector set to 150  C, the ion source to 230  C, and the transfer line temperature to 280  C. The scanning method was selected ion monitoring (SIM) mode.

Based on the self-constructed MWGC database (Metware Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China), mass spectrometry was used to identify the volatile compounds. The raw data after mass spectrometry analysis were processed by MassHunter software for qualitative and quantitative analysis. In addition, the relative content of each metabolite was calculated using an internal standard semiquantitative approach.
OAV and ROAV calculations

The odor threshold of volatile compounds was based on previous reports and Fenaroli's Handbook of Flavor Ingredients. The odor activity values (OAV) were calculated.where Ci and OTi are the relative content and aroma threshold of the volatile compounds in water, respectively.
ROAV was calculated with reference to.where Ci and Ti are the relative content and the threshold value of the compound I and Tmax/Cmax is the maximum of Ti/Ci ratio among all compounds in the sample.
Statistical analysis

Microsoft Office Excel 2016 was used to manage data. The principal component analysis (PCA) and veen were analyzed based on the Metware Cloud (https://cloud.metware.cn). The OPLS-DA analysis was performed using SIMCA 14.1 software to calculate the variable importance in projection (VIP). Duncan's test (P < 0.05) of SPSS 26.0 software was used to evaluate the significance of difference in metabolites between RT and DT. The heatmaps were drawn by TBtools software. VOCs with VIP >= 1, FDR < 0.05, and fold change >=2 were significantly changed volatile compounds (SCVs).
Results and discussion
Sensory evaluation and changes in moisture content during the scenting process of jasmine tea

To describe the flavor and aroma changes of two jasmine tea varieties during the scenting processes, sensory evaluation was conducted to analyze the flavor quality and difference of Jasminum sambac cv. 'Round leaf' tea (RT), double-petal Jasminum sambac cv. Bifoliatum tea (DT), and base tea (BT) (Fig. 1B and Supplemental Table S1). Their fragrance became more intense with an increase in the scenting process, and there were obvious differences in taste and aroma between RT and DT. In terms of taste, RT was smoother and softer than DT. In terms of aroma, RT was more elegant, fresh and lovely than DT. In addition, to evaluate and compare whether the aroma of jasmine is distorted and the spitting fragrance effect of jasmine tea after scenting, and we conducted sensory evaluations on two varieties of jasmine flowers (Supplemental Table S2). The color of 'Round leaf' jasmine flowers changed from white to slightly yellowish and reddish after scenting. The fragrance of its flowers was strong, lasting, fresh and lovely, but after scenting, the aroma decreased significantly and gave off a slightly fermented odor.

Moisture content is an indicator to regulate the moderation of jasmine tea. The moisture content of 'Round leaf' and double-petal jasmine flowers before jasmine tea fermentation was 85.39 % and 84.47 %, respectively. The moisture content of jasmine tea showed a gradually increasing trend with the scenting times (Supplemental Table S3).
Changes in free amino acids, catechins, and purine alkaloids during the scenting process of jasmine tea varieties

The free amino acid compounds of RT and DT and BT were analyzed by HPLC, detecting 19 compounds. Amino acids play significant roles in shaping the flavor profile of green tea by reducing its bitterness and astringency while enhancing its refreshing characteristics. As shown in Supplemental Table S4, with increasing the scenting process, the free amino acid content of the two types of jasmine tea exhibited little change, however, the RT content was higher than the DT content during scenting process. It may explain why RT tastes more mellow and delicate than DT. Theanine is the most characteristic nonprotein amino acid in tea, and it is the main source of the umami flavor of tea. The relative content of theanine in RT increased during the scenting process of jasmine tea and was higher than that of DT. It may be that the weak side chains in the protein structure were more prone to hydrolysis and pyrolysis with increasing temperature, forming free amino acids and increasing their content. There was no significant change in the caffeine content of jasmine tea with S1 and S5.
TAV analysis of the taste compounds of jasmine tea.
Table 1

TAVs are often utilized to measure the contribution of taste compounds. When TAV > 1, the compound contributes to taste. In this study, we calculated TAVs of 22 non-volatile compounds (Table 1). The TAV values of seven free amino acids, five catechins, and one alkaloid were > 1. It demonstrated that Asp>Thea> Glu > Arg > His>Val > Asn, which were free amino acids with TAV > 1, can be identified as the main taste amino acids of jasmine tea. In particular, Asp, Thea, and Glu, which present an umami taste, were higher than DT in RT, contributing to the smooth and soft flavors of RT.
Multivariate analysis of VOCs in jasmine tea and base tea during the scenting process

Volatile compounds profiles of jasmine tea and its basic tea. A. Diagram of volatile compounds in jasmine tea. A color represents a class of compounds. The length of the column represents the relative content value of the compounds. The innermost circle is the ratio of the quantity of each type of compounds to the total quantity of all compounds. B. PCA analysis. C. The total relative content of volatile compounds. D. The JTF index of jasmine tea during the different scenting process. E. Relative abundance of volatile compounds. F. Relative content of volatile compounds. H. Bean plot showing a comparison of the distribution of all the volatile categories in the two varieties. I. Heat map of relative content of top 8 volatile compounds.
Fig. 2

HS-SPME-GC-MS method was used to analyze RT, DT and BT. A total of 455 volatile compounds (VOCs) were detected, including 120 terpenoids, 93 esters, 53 heterocyclic compounds, 37 ketones, 42 hydrocarbons, 43 alcohols, and among others. Terpenoids and lipids had the highest number of VOCs, accounting for 26.37 % and 20.44 %, respectively (Fig. 2A). Principal component analysis (PCA) indicated that the contributions of PC1 and PC2 were 50.32 % and 24.36 %, respectively, with the first two principal components contributing more than 74 %. The jasmine tea and base tea exhibited obvious separation trends (Fig. 2B). The total content of VOCs in jasmine tea was significantly higher than that in base tea, and it showed an upward trend with increasing the scenting process. Before the fourth scenting process, the VOCs content in RT consistently exceeded that in DT. Moreover, the VOC content of RT exhibited a tendency toward saturation during the fourth scenting process, which may be attributed to the saturation of the adsorption capacity of BT for the 'Round leaf' jasmine flowers. After the fifth scenting process, the relative contents of RT and DT reached 4575.76 +- 71.39 mug/g and 5347.17 +- 217.56 mug/g, respectively (Fig. 2C).

JTF index was used to evaluate the aroma quality of jasmine tea, and the higher the JTF value, the higher the grade of jasmine tea. JTF index exhibited an upward trend from the first to fifth scenting process (Fig. 2D), which was consistent with the total content trend of aroma compounds. Although the total relative RT content was lower than that of DT at the fifth scenting process, JTF index of RT continued to be higher than that of DT during the scenting process, which may be due to the lower linalool content in RT at the fifth scenting times (Fig. 2I). It demonstrated that the aroma quality of RT was superior to that of DT, which was consistent with the sensory evaluation results.

Terpenoids and esters are the predominant volatile components of jasmine and jasmine tea. Esters represented the most abundant volatile component in jasmine tea, followed by terpenoids and alcohols. Their relative content increased with the increase of scenting times (Fig. 2E-F). It suggested that the aroma compounds of jasmine were effectively adsorbed into jasmine tea as the scenting process. The relative VOC content distribution profiles exhibited distinct differences between RT and DT during different scenting processes (Fig. 2H). The bean plot demonstrated that the relative RT content was higher than that of DT before the third scenting process. Tea aroma attributes are primarily determined by dominant aromatic compounds, not by the totality of volatile metabolites present. Based on the relative content, eight predominant aroma compounds were identified in jasmine tea, benzyl acetate, methyl phenylacetate, indole, methyl benzoate, methyl anthranilate, linalool, benzyl alcohol and cis-3-hexenyl benzoate (Fig. 2I).
The scenting process significantly increased the aroma of base tea

Volatile compounds comparative analysis among BT and jasmine tea (RT and DT). A. Volcano diagram of the significant changes volatile compounds (SCVs) in pairwise comparisons. B. Venn diagram analysis of differential volatile compounds. C. OPLS-DA score plot. D. Permutation tests plot. E. Circular packing diagram of volatile compounds (VIP > 1).
Fig. 3

To further explore whether the scenting process significantly improves the quality of base tea and identifies key aroma compounds in jasmine tea, the difference analysis was conducted for RT, DT, and BT. As shown in Fig. 3A, the number of significantly changed volatile compounds (SCVs) of DT increased with the increase of scenting times. In particular, DT5 vs BT has the largest number of SCVs, with 277 SCVs, including 242 up-regulated and 35 down-regulated. The number of up-regulated SCVs in RT4 vs BT was the largest, with 322 SCVs, including 228 up-regulated and 94 down-regulated (Fig. 3A). The Venn diagram were presented 185 SCVs in jasmine tea (RT and DT) and base tea (BT) (Fig. 3B).

Further OPLS-DA analysis of 185 SCVs revealed that it could effectively distinguish BT, RT and DT (R2X = 1, R2Y = 0.956 and Q2 = 0.89) (Figs. 3C). R2 and Q2 values close to 1 (Figs. 3D) indicate that the model fitting results were reliable. As a measure of variable importance, the VIP value reflects the extent to which each quality compound contributes to the model, with high values representing notable contributions. The SCVs with VIP > 1 significantly contribute to the classification. A total of 23 SCVs were determined from 185 SCVs based on the principle of VIP > 1 in the OPLS-DA model, to further screen the key aroma compounds of jasmine tea, including ten esters, seven terpenoids, four alcohols, one ketone and one heterocyclic compound (Fig. 3E).
The raincloud plot (A) and line chart of 23 volatile compounds with VIP > 1 (B).
Fig. 4

The quality of jasmine tea is affected by certain factors such as temperature, humidity, and other environmental conditions, which influence the release ability of jasmine flowers and the aroma absorption ability of the base tea, and modify the flavor and fragrance of the tea. The quality of jasmine tea is predominantly determined by its aroma, and is limited by factors such as the quality of jasmine flowers and the scenting process. In addition, the aroma profile of jasmine tea is predominantly shaped by the scenting process, which is a critical determinant of its flavor development. Linalool is a monoterpene alcohol, that imparts a floral and citrus-like odor. The relative content of terpenoids significantly increased after the first scenting process and increased with the scenting times, including linalool, alpha-muurolene, fenchone, beta-bisabolene, eremophilene, perillen and gamma-terpineol (Fig. 4A and B).

Esters such as benzyl acetate, methyl phenylacetate, methyl benzoate, methyl anthranilate, ethyl benzoate, (E)-3-hexenyl acetate, cis-3-hexenyl benzoate, cis-3-hexenyl butyrate and benzyl benzoate exhibited an overall upward trend of jasmine tea during the scenting process (Fig. 4A and B). Benzyl acetate, which has a floral and jasmine odor, was the most advantageous compound in terms of the relative content of jasmine tea. After the fifth scenting process, the relative content of benzyl acetate in RT and DT reached 1257.50 mug/g and 1384.61 mug/g, respectively, which were 298.69 and 328.88 times higher than BT. Methyl benzoate was described as a floral fragrance and was a key aroma compound in jasmine tea. Methyl anthranilate had a sweet, fruity grape-like odor and was a unique compound to jasmine tea. Meanwhile, cis-3-hexenyl benzoate has a fresh and green odor. Methyl salicylate is a volatile compound of amino acid derivatives, that can be formed by the enzymatic action of salicylate carboxymethyl transferase and the degradation of glycoside compounds. The relative content of methyl salicylate, which has the minty aroma of wintergreen, reached its peak at the first scenting stage and then gradually decreased.

The relative contents of 1-nonen-4-ol, benzeneethanol,alpha,alpha-dimethyl- and benzyl alcohol significantly accumulated during the jasmine scenting process, and exhibited similar change patterns (Fig. 4A and B). Benzyl alcohol provides a bitter almond-like, rose -like aroma. (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol exhibits a grassy and lettuce-like odor, and plays a notable role in shaping the fragrance of white tea. The relative content of (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol was higher in DT than in RT.

The same trend was observed for one ketone, which gradually increased during the scenting process, with a similar trend to that of most terpenoids (Fig. 4B). Indole provided a floral aroma, and its relative content was dominant in jasmine tea and continuously increased during the scenting process. Our previous study found that linalool, alpha-farnesene, methyl anthranilate, methyl salicylate, benzyl acetate and methyl benzoate were typical aroma compounds of jasmine. The results indicated that the primary volatile compounds in jasmine and jasmine tea were largely identical, and our research further confirms that jasmine tea aroma is predominantly developed during the scenting process. The scenting process significantly increased the content of aroma compounds in base tea.
Comparison of the VOCs of the two jasmine tea varieties during the scenting process

Volatile compound comparative analysis among RT and DT. A. Volcano diagram of the SCVs during the different scenting process in jasmine tea. B. OPLS-DA score plot. C. Permutation tests plot. D. Circular packing diagram of volatile compounds with VIP > 1. E. Cluster heatmap analysis of volatile compounds with VIP > 1 in the comparisons of RT and DT.
Fig. 5

We performed the differential analysis to compare the differences between RT and DT jasmine tea (Fig. 5A). It demonstrated that the aromas of RT and DT exhibited significant differences. Before the third scenting process, the number of SCVs up-regulated in RT vs DT exceeded those down-regulated, potentially enhancing the overall RT aroma. The number of differentially abundant compounds significantly increased from the fourth scenting, and the number of down-regulated compounds was significantly higher than the up-regulated compounds. In particular, after the fifth scenting process, 121 SCVs were detected in RT5 vs DT5, including 9 up-regulated and 112 down-regulated SCVs. The OPLS-DA analysis of 211 SCVs demonstrated that the method was effective in distinguishing between DT and RT (Fig. 5B-C). The distance between RT and DT in the first scenting process (RT1 and DT1) was relatively close. We identified 22 VOCs with VIP > 1 based on the OPLS-DA model, including seven esters, four terpenoids, four alcohols, three hydrocarbons, two aldehydes, one ketones and one phenol (Fig. 5D).

Cluster analysis was conducted using TBtools software on 22 significantly changed VOCs screened from jasmine tea (RT and DT) during the scenting processes (Fig. 5E). The relative content of Group I compounds was dominant in RT (RT > DT). A total of 10 compounds, including (E)-3- hexenyl acetate, benzyl benzoate, (E)-beta-ocimene, gamma-terpineol and benzeneacetaldehyde, played a significant role in shaping the RT aroma. The opposite phenomenon was observed in Group II compared with Group I (DT > RT). The eight compounds (eugenol, beta-damascenone, cis-3-hexenyl butyrate, (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol, (E)-2-hexenal, 4-hexen-3-one, methyl 2-methylaminobenzoate and alpha-acoradiene) modified the aroma of DT.
OAV and ROAV calculations for the potential key aroma compounds

The content level of aroma compounds can not be used as the basis to determine the tea aroma profile, because those with higher odor activity value (OAV) are usually assigned to the aroma characteristics of tea. When the OAV >= 1, it is considered that the aroma compound significantly contributes to the aroma. As shown in Supplemental Table S3, 46 volatile compounds with OAV >= 1 were identified, indicating that these compounds may significantly contribute to the jasmine tea aroma.

The relative concentrations corresponding to relative OAV (ROAV) combined the sensory thresholds of each volatile compound to quantitatively evaluate the degree of contribution of different VOCs to the overall aroma and identify the key aroma compounds of jasmine tea. The key aroma compound (ROAV>=1) determines most of the flavor of an aroma system. Within a defined quantitative range, a positive correlation was observed between the ROAV and the contribution of the compound to the overall aroma profile, where aroma-active compounds with ROAV values ranging from 0.1 to 1 demonstrated significant modifying effects on tea aroma characteristics.

passages.text: As shown in Table 2, a total of six key aroma compounds with ROAV>1 were identified from jasmine tea (RT and DT), namely, methyl anthranilate (sweet, fruity grape-like), benzyl acetate (fruity, fragrance), linalool (floral), indole (floral, naphthyl), methyl benzoate (fruity) and methyl salicylate (mint, wintergreen), which significantly contributed to the overall floral and sweet aroma characteristics of jasmine tea. The alpha-farnesene, with floral and herbaceous aromas, is the main aroma compound of jasmine flowers. It was incredible that although OAV > 1 of alpha-farnesene was observed during the different scenting processes of jasmine tea, ROAV was<0.1 in this study. The two aroma compounds, cis-3-hexenyl benzoate (fresh, green) and alpha-ionone (sweet, floral, violet-like), played vital roles in modifying the overall aroma of jasmine tea. Based on previous research on the aroma compounds of jasmine flowers, the characteristic aroma compounds of jasmine tea identified in this study demonstrated substantial concordance with the principal aroma compounds of jasmine flowers, indicating that the characteristic aroma compounds of jasmine tea were primarily attributed to the absorption of jasmine fresh flower aroma by the base tea during the scenting process.
Comprehensive analysis reveals the key aroma compounds of jasmine tea and the characteristic aromas of different varieties of jasmine tea

Comprehensive analysis reveals the key aroma compounds of jasmine tea and the characteristic aromas of different varieties of jasmine tea. A. The key aroma compounds of jasmine tea. B. The characteristic aroma compounds of DT. C. The characteristic aroma compounds of RT.
Fig. 6

Through the differential analysis (VIP > 1) and ROAV analysis, methyl anthranilate, benzyl acetate, linalool, indole, methyl benzoate and methyl salicylate were identified as the key aroma compounds in jasmine tea (RT and DT) (Fig. 6A). The (E)-3-hexenyl acetate (fruity, green), (E)-beta-ocimene (floral) and benzeneacetaldehyde (floral) were the characteristic aroma compounds that exhibited elegance, freshness and loveliness in RT (Fig. 6C), whereas (E)-2-hexenal (green, grassy), beta-damascenone (floral, rose-like), methyl 2-methylaminobenzoate (fruity), (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol (green) and eugenol (floral, clove-like) were the characteristic aroma compounds that exhibited strong and lasting fragrance in DT (Fig. 6B). It can greatly elucidate the flavor quality characteristics of RT and DT.
Conclusion

This study investigated the non-volatile and volatile compounds during the scenting process of jasmine tea. The scenting process can significantly improve the quality of the base tea, and the aroma level of jasmine tea increases with the increase of scenting times. The six key aroma compounds, namely methyl anthranilate, benzyl acetate, linalool, indole, methyl benzoate and methyl salicylate, were identified significantly contributed to the overall floral and sweet aroma characteristics of jasmine tea. We developed a new product, 'Round leaf' jasmine tea (RT), which reached better quality in the fourth scenting process. The characteristic aroma compounds of RT that exhibited elegance and freshness were (E)-3-hexenyl acetate, (E)-beta-ocimene and benzeneacetaldehyde. It contributes to enriching the production cultivar of jasmine tea and provides a scientific basis for the application of the new cultivar of 'Round leaf' jasmine in production.

passages.text: Systematic review and meta-analysis protocol of impact of pharmacist-led antibiotic stewardship audit-feedback intervention
This protocol outlines a rigorous plan for conducting a high-quality meta-analysis examining the impact of pharmacist-led audit and feedback interventions within antibiotic stewardship programs.
It details the full methodological framework, from topic selection through to the statistical approaches planned for data synthesis.

By publicly sharing our protocol through an academic publishing platform, we aim to promote transparency, invite constructive input, and contribute to raising the methodological standards for meta-analyses in the domain of antibiotic stewardship.

The rise of resistance to antibiotic agents continues to present a substantial challenge to healthcare systems. In response, antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) have been widely endorsed as a core strategy to promote the responsible use of antimicrobials and to curb the progression of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Pharmacist-led audit and feedback interventions hold significant promise due to pharmacists' clinical expertise and direct role in optimizing antimicrobial prescribing. However, despite their potential, the current body of evidence evaluating the effectiveness of pharmacist-led audit and feedback within ASPs remains limited and fragmented. A clearer understanding of their impact is essential to inform policy decisions, support broader implementation, and enhance the overall effectiveness of stewardship efforts. This protocol has been registered with the PROSPERO under the registration number CRD420251036088. The review will be conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines.A comprehensive search will be carried out across four major databases, and studies will be selected based on clearly defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The risk of bias in the included studies will be assessed using Cochrane riak of bias assessment tools. Publication bias will be examined using funnel plots and Egger's test. For the quantitative synthesis, a random-effects model will be employed.

Specifications table
Background

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most critical global health threats of the 21st century, with far-reaching implications for public health, economic development, and the sustainability of modern medical practices. The rise of resistant pathogens compromises the efficacy of essential treatments, leading to prolonged illnesses, increased healthcare costs, and elevated mortality rates. In 2021 alone, AMR was associated with an estimated 4.71 million deaths worldwide, underscoring the urgent need for coordinated global action. Projections indicate that if current trends persist, AMR could contribute to approximately 169 million deaths between 2025 and 2050, potentially reversing decades of progress in infectious disease control and threatening the effectiveness of routine surgical procedures, cancer therapies, and critical care interventions.

Antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) are recognized as one of the cornerstone strategies in the global effort to combat AMR, as they are designed to promote the judicious use of antibiotics through evidence-based prescribing practices. These programs aim to optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing the unintended consequences of antimicrobial use, including resistance, toxicity, and unnecessary healthcare costs. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) strongly advocates for the inclusion of pharmacists as key leaders in the implementation and management of ASPs, given their expertise in pharmacotherapy and their critical role in influencing prescribing behaviors. Despite this recommendation, there remains a limited body of consolidated evidence evaluating the specific impact of pharmacist-led audit and feedback interventions within ASPs on antibiotic utilization. Furthermore, the mechanisms through which pharmacists contribute to improved prescribing:particularly via audit and feedback strategies:are not yet fully understood. This gap underscores the need for high-quality, systematic evaluation to determine the effectiveness of such interventions and to guide future integration of pharmacists into antimicrobial stewardship efforts.

passages.text: This protocol forms the methodological foundation for a forthcoming systematic literature review and meta-analysis aimed at evaluating the impact of pharmacist-led audit and feedback interventions within ASP. By establishing a transparent and structured approach in advance, this protocol ensures methodological rigor, minimizes the risk of bias, and enhances the reproducibility of the review. The primary objective is to synthesize current evidence on how pharmacist-led audit-feedback influences antibiotic prescribing practices, with the broader goal of informing policy, clinical decision-making, and future research in antimicrobial stewardship.
Description of protocol
Protocol registration

To ensure transparency and methodological rigor in the conduct of this systematic review and meta-analysis, a protocol summary has been registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD420251036088. The review will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A graphical abstract is included to visually summarize the methodological framework of the study.
Research question
Patient: Patient on antibiotics
Intervention: Integration of audit and feedback intervention for antibiotic prescribing with pharmacist involvement
Comparison: Without audit and feedback intervention for antibiotic prescribing with pharmacist involvement

Outcome: Primary outcome: Days of therapy per (100/1000) patient days. Secondary outcome: appropriate prescribing, mortality, antibiotic resistance, infection recurrence rates, or length of hospital stay.

The research question guiding this systematic review and meta-analysis will be structured using the PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome), which provides a clear and systematic approach for defining the key elements of the review. The components of the PICO framework applied in this study are as follows:
Search strategy

A systematic literature search will be conducted across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, EBSCO/CINAHL, and Web of Science, to identify relevant peer-reviewed studies. The search will be restricted to publications from January 1, 2000, to June 31, 2024. A combination of predefined keywords and Boolean operators (e.g., "AND," "OR") will be employed to optimize the retrieval of pertinent literature. The full search strategy is detailed in Supplementary Material 1.

Studies published in English that assess the impact of pharmacist involvement in antibiotic stewardship audit and feedback interventions will be included, based on the eligibility criteria outlined in Table 1.
Data screening and extraction
PRISMA flow diagram.
Figure 1:

The screening process will be conducted in two stages. Initially, one reviewer will screen the titles and abstracts of all retrieved records, followed by full-text assessment for potentially eligible studies. A second reviewer will independently verify the screening and eligibility decisions. Any discrepancies between the reviewers will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer, if necessary. All records retrieved from the databases will be imported into EndNote 21 reference management software for the identification and removal of duplicates. A manual verification will also be performed to ensure the thorough elimination of duplicate entries. The overall study selection process will be documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1). Data from all eligible studies will be extracted and managed using Microsoft Excel (16.95.1).
Quality assessment

The risk of bias for included studies will be assessed using Cochrane tools based on study design. For cohort studies, case-control studies, and quasi-experimental designs, the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I V2) tool will be applied. For randomized controlled trials, the Risk of Bias (RoB 2) tool will be used. The ROBINS-I tool evaluates risk of bias across seven key domains: confounding, classification of interventions, selection of participants, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selection of the reported result. Each domain is assessed through a structured set of signalling questions designed to elicit detailed information about the study and its analytical approach. Once all relevant questions are answered, a predefined algorithm integrates the responses to generate an overall risk of bias judgement for each domain. These judgements are categorized as low, moderate, serious, or critical risk of bias, reflecting the extent to which bias may affect the study's results. The RoB 2 tool offers a structured framework for assessing the risk of bias in the results of randomized trials. It encompasses five domains that address potential sources of bias arising from: the randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Each domain includes a series of signalling questions designed to guide reviewers in evaluating the trial's methodological rigor and to inform domain-level and overall risk of bias judgments. To visually present the risk of bias assessments, traffic-light plots will be generated using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Visualization (Robvis) tool. Publication bias will be assessed through visual inspection of funnel plots, complemented by Egger's regression test. A p-value of less than 0.05 will be considered indicative of significant publication bias.
Data analysis

A qualitative synthesis will be undertaken to systematically organize and summarize key characteristics of the included studies. This synthesis will capture information such as author, year of publication, study design, setting, population, scope, intervention characteristics (e.g delivary mode, frequency, duration), Feedback team characteristics (e.g, specialty, experience), sample size, and measure (e.g days of therapy, length of hospital stay, mortality).

For the quantitative analysis, a random-effects meta-analysis model will be applied using R software (version 4.4.1) and RStudio (version 2024.09.0+375). To ensure comparability across studies, antibiotic use will be standardized as days of therapy per 100 patient-days (DOT/100 patient-days). Statistical heterogeneity among the included studies will be assessed using the I2 statistic and interpreted in accordance with the guidelines provided in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Heterogeneity will be categorized as follows: low (<40%), moderate (30%-60%), substantial (50%-90%), and considerable (>75%). These overlapping thresholds reflect the contextual nature of heterogeneity interpretation, considering both the magnitude and consistency of effects across studies. In the presence of substantial heterogeneity, subgroup analyses will be conducted to explore potential sources of variability. These analyses will stratify the results based on study design, geographic region, and healthcare setting. Sensitivity analyses will be conducted using the leave-one-out method and prediction intervals to assess the robustness of the findings.

Limitations

A limitation of this study is that it focuses in the inclusion of only studies published in the English language. While this approach ensures consistency in data interpretation and quality assessment, it may introduce language bias and limit the comprehensiveness of the evidence base. Relevant studies published in other languages could have been excluded, potentially omitting valuable data and perspectives from non-English-speaking regions. As a result, the findings may not fully reflect global practices or outcomes related to pharmacist-led antibiotic stewardship interventions.

passages.text: Amino acid-based risk stratification model improves prognostic precision in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. We hope to provide a new conceptual basis for evaluating patient prognosis and guiding diagnosis and treatment. Twenty patients newly diagnosed with DLBCL were selected as the experimental group, and 10 healthy volunteers composed the control group. The expression of amino acids in the plasma of patients and healthy controls was detected via liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). The sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis (sPLS-DA) model was established. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed on the selected differential amino acids. Tryptophan and glutamine, are significantly correlated with prognosis, which can be used as potential DLBCL biomarkers. MATLAB was used to create a partial least squares regression (PLSR) prognostic model and a support vector regression (SVR) machine learning prognostic model. The R2of the PLSR model is 0.33, and the RMSE is 14.22. A paired - sample T - test was conducted on the predicted values and the actual values, with P = 0.999. The R2 of the SVR model is 0.89, the MAE is 1.95, and the MBE is 0.77. After training, the PLSR prognostic model and SVR machine can predict the prognosis of DLBCL and provide convenient guidance for the treatment of DLBCL.
Background

About 25% of all lymphoma cases are DLBCL, making it the biggest non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) subgroup. DLBCL has been classified into at least two distinct molecular subtypes based on gene expression analysis: germinal center B-cell like (GCB) DLBCL and non-germinal center B-cell like (non-GCB) DLBCL, and compared to individuals with the GCB subtype, those with the non-GCB subtype had a noticeably worse overall survival (OS). The first-line treatment for DLBCL patients at the moment is rituximab plus CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin and its liposomes, vincristine, glucocorticoids), which significantly increases patient survival rates. However, many patients with DLBCL respond poorly to this treatment, greatly affecting efficacy. Hematologists have undertaken numerous novel approaches for the first-line treatment of DLBCL. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) has developed evidence-based recommendations for cancer treatment, which are adopted by healthcare providers globally. As an additional first-line recommendation for immunochemotherapy, Pola-R-CHP (Polatuzumab vedotin-piiq (Polivy), rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone)is also widely utilized in the routine management of DLBCL. As the exploration of the mechanisms underlying DLBCL progresses and pharmaceutical manufacturing processes continue to improve, an increasing number of novel therapies have been introduced into clinical practice. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are therapeutic agents utilized for cell-specific chemotherapy. These compounds function by binding to a protein on the surface of cancer cells, subsequently internalizing into the cellular environment. Upon entering the cell, the chemotherapeutic agent is released. Currently, ADCs targeting CD19, CD79b, and CD30 proteins have been successfully applied in clinical settings. Immunotherapy is a form of pharmacological treatment that enhances the activity of the immune system. It can be administered as a monotherapy or in combination with other types of therapy. Monoclonal antibody therapies targeting CD19 and CD20, as well as bispecific antibodies capable of simultaneously binding two distinct proteins (CD20 and CD3) to recruit T cells for cancer treatment, have undergone extensive clinical trials and applications. Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy involves extracting T cells from a patient and modifying these cells by adding a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), thereby training the patient's own immune cells to combat lymphoma. It is important to note that CAR-T cell therapy, as well as bispecific antibody therapy, is not suitable for everyone and may elicit severe, sometimes life-threatening, reactions. For patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is also a viable treatment option. However, this decision should be made with great caution, as there is a potential for extremely severe side effects that could even be life-threatening. Despite the usefulness of cells of origin for predicting prognosis, the GCB and non-GCB subtypes are still heterogeneous, with good and poor prognostic subgroups within each group. The heterogeneity of DLBCL, like several other types of cancer, is thought to be caused by different patterns of dysregulation of cell signaling pathways caused by some abnormalities. Different mutation profiles lead to abnormal expression of amino acids encoded by genes in tumors, resulting in altered energy metabolism in tumor cells. This can improve the survival and reproductive ability of tumor cells and lead to poor prognosis. Currently, an increasing number of researchers are attempting to identify specific energy metabolism pathways related to DLBCL and provide ideas for developing new biomarkers that can predict patient prognosis.

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins and essential components in various life processes. They are crucial in specific physiological functions, including metabolism, nerve signaling, and the transport of liposomes. They generate energy through intermediate metabolites to fuel other biosynthetic pathways. Research has demonstrated that hematological malignancies often depend on certain amino acids for survival, and a shortage of these amino acids heightens metabolic weaknesses, creating more possibilities for treatment. Some amino acid-targeting enzymes that have been approved for the treatment of hematological tumors have shown promising results. The use of metabolomics to quantitatively analyze amino acids in biological samples has played an important role in the diagnosis of blood system diseases and the study of growth and development mechanisms.

To the best of our knowledge, the prognostic or predictive role of plasma metabolomics in DLBCL has not been elucidated. At present, the main prognostic tool used for risk stratification of DLBCL patients in clinical practice is the clinic-based international prognostic index (IPI). The higher the IPI score is, the worse the prognosis of patients. However, the index seems less effective in pinpointing individual high-risk patients, making it necessary to have reliable biomarkers for identifying these patients.

In this study, plasma samples from newly diagnosed DLBCL patients and healthy controls were collected, and the prognosis of newly diagnosed DLBCL patients was evaluated in combination with basic clinical conditions. Based on the evaluation results, patients were categorized into mild and severe groups. Additionally, amino acids in plasma samples were analyzed using LC-MS/MS through the Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) method, and appropriate statistical methods were applied to assess differences in amino acid metabolism between the groups. Moreover, metabolic pathway analysis of differential amino acids significantly affecting prognosis was performed to identify metabolic pathways related to prognosis and to provide researchers with new options to identify new mechanisms and pathways related to the diagnosis and treatment of DLBCL. Our primary objective was to identify distinct amino acid metabolites that could serve as new biomarkers for predicting DLBCL. We did this by combining the critical amino acids and clinical indications to create a plausible prognosis prediction model. This procedure not only confirms the function of differential amino acid metabolites as biomarkers but also offers a model for prognosticating DLBCL.
Methods
Research subjects and sample collection methods

Peripheral blood samples were collected from 20 patients diagnosed with DLBCL at the Department of Hematology of Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to Shandong First Medical University from January 2020 to May 2021 and 10 healthy volunteers. All patients were diagnosed for the first time and never received any treatment. The control group was composed of healthy volunteers with normal laboratory results during the same period. Patients provided informed consent, and essential information:including sex, age, general condition, tumor immunohistochemistry results, tumor stage, and IPI was documented. Risk stratification was conducted based on patients' clinical data. Specifically, risk stratification is carried out based on the calculated IPI score of patients. In the IPI prognostic model, when there are risk factors such as age over 60 years old, Ann Arbor - Cotswolds stage from III to IV, more than one extranodal involvement site, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) exceeding the normal value, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score greater than 1 point, each risk factor is scored 1 point and added up to obtain the final IPI score. The low risk group has an IPI score of 0-1 point, the low to medium risk group and the moderate to high risk group have scores of 2 points and 3 points respectively, and the high - risk group has a score of 4-5 points. Two milliliters of fasting venous blood was collected from all the subjects in the morning, and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) was used for anticoagulation. Let the blood samples stand for about 10-20 min. This effectively allows more time for the air bubbles introduced during the blood - drawing process in the samples to rise to the surface of the tube, thereby reducing the risk of inhaling air bubbles during pipetting and ensuring a higher quality of the transferred plasma. Subsequently, the samples were centrifuged at 1006 g for 10 min. The supernatant (plasma) was stored at -80  C until analysis.
Sample information
Sample information: There were two groups of blood samples. Ten biological samples from a healthy control group and 20 biological samples from a DLBCL group were used (see Table 1 for details).
