Sequencing methods for 20 amino acids in DLBCL
Targeted metabolomics analysis of the plasma amino acid profiles of DLBCL patients and controls was performed via the LC-MS/MS method, and 20 common amino acids in the plasma were quantified.
Standard curve

The standard substance was diluted with water into a standard working solution of serial concentrations, and the standard curve solution was prepared according to to 2) to establish the labeling curve.
Metabolite extraction

The plasma samples were thawed at room temperature and analyzed via LC-MS/MS. A total of 100 microL of blood was collected, and precooled methanol (Merck, 144282)/acetonitrile (Merck, 1499230-935) (1:1, V/V) was added. The mixture was vortexed, mixed for 30 s, left for 10 min, and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm at 4  C for 10 min. The supernatant was then removed to a polypropylene sample tube and dried under nitrogen gas. A total of 1000 microL of water was used to redissolve the supernatant, and the solution was filtered and injected. A mixture of all the samples was prepared as a quality control (QC) sample.
Chromatographic mass spectrometry analysis

Sample separation was conducted using a Nexera X2 LC-30AD HPLC system (Shimadzu). A quality control (QC) sample was included at regular intervals among experimental samples to assess system stability and reproducibility, while a standard amino acid metabolite mixture was used within the sample set to adjust chromatographic retention times.

Mass spectrometry analysis was carried out on a 5500 QTRAP mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) in positive ion mode. Conditions for the 5500 QTRAP ESI source were: source temperature at 500  C; ion source gas 1 (GS1): 50; ion source gas 2 (GS2): 50; curtain gas (CUR): 35; and ion spray voltage (IS): 5500 V. Targeted ion pairs were analyzed in MRM mode.
Data analysis

Chromatographic peak areas and retention times were extracted using Analyst and SCIEX OS software. Amino acid standards were applied to adjust retention times for accurate metabolite identification. Equal portions of all samples were combined to form QC samples, allowing evaluation of data stability and reproducibility.
Bioinformatics analysis method of amino acid sequencing screening results

Amino acid sequencing results and clinical data were further analyzed. During the analysis process, MetaboAnalyst, SIMCA - P software, and R were applied. Multivariate statistical methods, including principal component analysis (PCA) and sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis (sPLS-DA), were employed to perform dimensionality reduction on the multidimensional data while retaining as much original information as possible. PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that aims to project high-dimensional data onto a low-dimensional space while retaining as much of the data's variation information as possible. PCA transforms the original variables into a new set of uncorrelated variables through linear transformation, known as principal components. The first principal component captures the largest amount of information variation in the data, and subsequent principal components capture the remaining variation in turn. Meanwhile, sPLS-DA is designed to handle high-dimensional data with numerous independent variables, which is particularly common in the fields of biology and medicine. It selects the most discriminative features by introducing sparsity constraints and conducts classification analysis simultaneously. PCA can effectively reduce the dimensionality of amino acid sequencing data for subsequent analysis and visualization. After applying PCA, the data can be simplified into several principal components, providing a clear input structure for subsequent analyses such as sPLS-DA. sPLS-DA has a powerful feature selection ability, capable of screening out variables that make the most significant contributions to classification from numerous independent variables, which is particularly important in detecting differential metabolites. Meanwhile, by combining dimensionality reduction and classification, sPLS-DA can improve accuracy while reducing the complexity of the model, making the discovery of clinically relevant information more reliable. In the biomedical field, data are usually high-dimensional and noisy. The combination of PCA and sPLS-DA can reduce the interference of noise while retaining important information, laying a foundation for subsequent bioinformatics analysis and screening of differential metabolites. Differential metabolites were then identified and analyzed. The metabolites responsible for distinguishing the severe DLBCL group from the mild DLBCL group were the metabolites that were statistically significant according to multivariate analysis (VIP > 1.0 and P < 0.05).
Sample selection
DLBCL 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, and 20 were selected, resulting in a total of 17 samples.
For categorical labels, 12 were mild, and 45 were severe.
Spectral-effect correlation analysis

Clinical and mass spectrometry variables were selected. PCA was used first to preview the data distribution of all sample points, and then sPLS-DA was used to model and analyze the data to explore the mathematical relationship between amino acid profiles and clinical prognostic values.
The VIP value, also called variable projection importance, represents the contribution of each metabolite ion to the block. The higher the VIP value is, the stronger the correlation.
Permutation test

The sample labels (mild and severe cases) were randomly shuffled 100 times, the average Euclidean distance of the two groups of samples after clustering was calculated, and the distance of the real data was used as the denominator for standardization. The p value is the number of times/100 that the mean distance was greater than the true data in the random case.
Cluster heatmap analysis
Cluster heatmaps were drawn via hierarchical clustering, with colors from blue to red representing the content of the associated amino acids from low to high.
Bubble map analysis of pathway enrichment
KEGG annotation and pathway analysis were performed on the screened differential metabolites, and the key metabolic pathways of differential metabolite mapping were retrieved via enrichment analysis.
Data analysis

SPSS 18.0 statistical analysis software was used to analyze the experimental data. The measurement data are expressed as the means +- standard deviations (means +- SDs), and univariate analysis was performed via a t test. For multivariate analysis, linear regression was performed using multiple groups of amino acids with specific characteristics, and stepwise regression was performed via the backward method; P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Establishment of prognostic models
Selection of variables for the prognostic models

The incorporation of tumor molecular characteristics and the microenvironment into the IPI can better guide prognostic analysis. The key clinical information and pivotal amino acids of the 20 patients were included as input variables in the prognostic model. PFS, gathered through reviewing patients' treatment records and follow-up calls, was used as the output variable.
Selection of prognostic model variables

MATLAB was used to randomly split the dataset into training and test sets. The PLSR model was fit with training data and predicted with test data, and the predictive correlation coefficient was calculated. On the basis of the validation results, the latent variables or other parameters are adjusted, and the training and validation steps are repeated to improve the model prediction accuracy.
Construction and operation of the SVR machine learning model

MATLAB is used to divide the dataset into training and test sets, an appropriate kernel function is chosen, and the SVR model is built with the fitrsvm function in MATLAB. Cross-validation is employed for automatic hyperparameter tuning to enhance model performance. The SVR model is trained with the training dataset and predicted with the test dataset, predictive performance metrics are calculated, model performance is analyzed, parameters are adjusted, and the training and evaluation processes are iterated to achieve optimal performance (Fig. 1).

Quantitative analysis of plasma amino acids in patients with DLBCL

A total of 20 kinds of amino acids were detected in the QC samples, and the quantitative results of the amino acid analysis are shown in Table 2. The RSDs of the tested substances in the QC samples were all less than 30%, indicating that our data had reliable stability. According to the detailed quantitative data of amino acids in the samples, a box plot of patients and healthy controls was drawn (Fig. 9 - 1). The clustering heatmap of metabolites in positive ion mode is shown in Fig. 9 - 2, which compares the distribution characteristics of amino acid quantitative data between patients and healthy controls. We can clearly see that the expression of eight amino acids in the plasma of DLBCL patients is significantly different from that of normal healthy controls. Among them, Asp, Glu, Phe, and Thr showed an upward trend in DLBCL. Gly, His, Ser, and Trp showed a downward trend in DLBCL, as shown in Fig. 9 - 3, and the differences were statistically significant (P < 0.05).

Establishment of a model to analyze the relationship between amino acid expression and clinical prognosis

The amino acid expression and clinical characteristics of patients were used as variables. On the basis of PCA, the mass spectrometry data obtained from the experiment and the clinical data were used to establish a supervised sPLS-DA model, which revealed that patients with differential amino acid expression and poor clinical prognostic factors also had poor prognoses (Fig. 2). SPLS-DA can force the regression coefficients of variables with small effects to zero, which is better in this set of data, indirectly indicating that many variables do not play a role in classification. The basic characteristics and clinically relevant data of the 20 patients are shown in Table 3.
Mass spectrum + clinical + sPLS-DA analysis

The figure illustrates the results of models constructed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (sPLS-DA), aimed at highlighting differences between patients' amino acid expression profiles and their clinical characteristics. Green points represent severe patients (with IPI scores of 4-5), while red points denote the remaining mild patients. In the two-dimensional score plot on the left, the X-axis represents Principal Component 1 (explaining 20.9% of the variance), and the Y-axis represents Principal Component 2 (explaining 8.5% of the variance). The two groups exhibit a clear separation, clustering in distinct regions, indicating significant differences in amino acid expression profiles between the two patient groups. This distinction is closely associated with patient prognosis and clinical features. The three-dimensional scatter plot on the right further elucidates the differences between patient groups. On this plot, the X-axis again represents Principal Component 1 (explaining 20.9% of the variance), the Y-axis represents Principal Component 2 (8.5% of the variance), and the Z-axis represents Principal Component 3 (6.9% of the variance). The three-dimensional visualization clearly delineates the green and red points with minimal overlap, demonstrating distinct patterns across multiple principal components. This further supports the reliability and validity of the PCA and sPLS-DA results. In summary, these analytical findings indicate that differences in amino acid expression are closely related to patients' clinical characteristics, potentially providing valuable biomarkers for prognostic evaluation.

Analysis of differential amino acid metabolic pathways related to the prognosis of patients

Pathway analysis was performed for the two amino acids that significantly affected the prognostic grouping, and the pathway enrichment bubble plots obtained from the analysis are shown in Fig. 6. Three metabolic pathways appear to be most strongly linked to patient prognosis, as they showed the highest number of enriched metabolites. These pathways include D-glutamine and D-glutamate metabolism, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis, and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism. KEGG analysis was applied to examine D-Gln and D-Glu metabolism, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis, as well as alanine, aspartic acid, and glutamate metabolism. Notably, metabolites encompass not only tryptophan and glutamine themselves but also all compounds involved in the reaction steps of their metabolic processes, regardless of whether they serve as initial substrates. These compounds were obtained from the KEGG database and subjected to alignment and enrichment analysis against known metabolic pathways.

Higher values indicate a more substantial impact of the pathway. The Y-axis represents the significance level of the pathway, expressed as the negative logarithm (base 10) of the p-value (-log10(P)), where higher numerical values denote stronger enrichment significance. The size of each bubble indicates the number of metabolites involved in the respective pathway, with larger bubbles signifying a greater number of metabolites, thereby emphasizing the importance of that pathway. The color gradient of the bars represents the p-values, ranging from red (high significance) to yellow (low significance). Longer bars indicate higher enrichment ratios, reflecting the relative importance of amino acids within those pathways.
Construction the prognostic model
Selection of prognostic model variables

The identified differential amino acids in plasma, tryptophan and glutamine, are significantly correlated with prognosis and are included as important independent variables (input variables) in the prognostic model. Clinical data such as the IPI score, grouping, age, number of extranodal sites, and LDH level were also included as independent variables in the prognostic model. In our study, the follow-up duration for patient DLBCL12 was from the onset of the disease until death, which was 15 months. The follow-up duration for the other participants was calculated from the onset of the disease to the study cutoff date (May 2024). The median follow-up time is 39 months (range: 15-53 months). During this period, all patients except patient 12 remained alive and completed the follow-up. The final dataset of variables is shown in Table 4.

PLSR prognostic model

A PLSR prognostic model was established via MATLAB, with repeated training and validation steps, and the prognostic expression for PFS is derived as follows: PFS = 110.2092 + (-5.5576) * Gln + (-6.7974) * Trp + 0.1395 * Age + 3.1042 * Number of extranodal sites + 0.0047 * Number of LDH + (-7.2143) * Number of IPI risk stratifications + (-2.8840) * IPI score. Operation attempts enable individualized PFS prediction. We validated the predictive capability of the PLSR prognostic model (Fig. 7). The scatter plot on the left-hand side elucidates the relationship between the actual values and the predicted values obtained through PLS regression. Although the distribution of data points in the plot exhibits slight dispersion, it also indicates the model's capability to predict the output values. To further validate the predictive ability of the model, we conducted a residual analysis, which is presented in the right-hand side figure. It displays the differences (residuals) between predicted and actual values, with a blue dashed line representing the zero-residual line. Most residuals are distributed within a range close to zero, suggesting that the overall error of the model is relatively small. The absence of apparent systematic bias or trends in the residuals indicates that the model fitting does not exhibit significant issues.
Validation of the Predictive Capability of the PLSR Prognostic Model

The left figure presents a comparison between the actual and predicted values of the PLSR prognostic model. The x-axis represents the standardized actual Y values (Actual Y), which are the observed outcomes. The y-axis represents the standardized predicted Y values (Predicted Y), which are the outcomes predicted by the model. Each yellow dot corresponds to a pair of actual and predicted values for a given data point. The red dashed line denotes the ideal fit line (Ideal Fit), indicating the scenario where actual values perfectly match the predicted values. The right figure illustrates a residual analysis. The x-axis represents the sample index (Sample Index), which is the identifier for different samples. The y-axis represents the residuals, which are the differences between the predicted and actual values. Each scatter point indicates the residual value for a specific sample. The blue dashed line signifies the zero residual line (Zero Residual Line), representing the ideal level of residuals for the model.

To further verify the validation ability of the PLSR model, we calculated the coefficient of determination (R2) of the model to be 0.33 and the root mean square error (RMSE) to be 14.22. Meanwhile, we conducted a paired - sample T - test on the predicted values and actual values of the model. The results showed that P = 0.999, confirming that there was no significant difference between the predicted values and the actual values. When exploring the reasons for the relatively large RMSE and low R2 of the PLSR prediction model, we considered that PLSR establishes a linear relationship through projection and dimensionality reduction, and there may be a non - linear association between PFS and other independent variables. Its linear assumption may lead to under - fitting. Therefore, we subsequently constructed an SVR model.
SVR machine learning prognostic model

An SVR machine learning model was developed via MATLAB, with a 75% sample ratio (n = 15) for the training set and the remaining samples for the test set, achieving good model training parameters (Figs. 8). The input parameter features can predict the PFS and provide prediction accuracy and confidence intervals. Subsequently, we tested the predictive ability of the model. The R2was 0.89, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) was 1.95, and the Mean Bias Error (MBE) was 0.77. Overall, the R2 and MAE values of the SVR model indicate good predictive ability. An R2 value close to 1 suggests that the model performs well in capturing the variability of the data, while the MAE gives a relatively low prediction error.

Discussion

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) ranks among the top ten causes of cancer mortality. DLBCL is the most common form of NHL, accounting for around 30-40% of cases globally. Patients often present with rapidly enlarging tumors in single or multiple nodes or extranodal locations. According to the NCCN guidelines, these large, fast-growing tumors are frequently found in the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone marrow, or other tissues and organs, with symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Current screening for lymphoma involves imaging techniques, such as PET-CT and ultrasound, with clinical diagnoses confirmed through histopathological biopsy. Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry help classify lymphoma type and cell origin, though these methods do not allow for early, rapid diagnosis or prognosis evaluation of DLBCL.

To simplify the diagnostic process of DLBCL and achieve accurate and rapid prediction of DLBCL prognosis, researchers have done a great deal of work and established various prognostic prediction models from different perspectives. Researchers such as Zhang started from the existing tumor marker IQ motif-containing GTPase activating protein (IQGAP) 2. Inspired by its predictive role in hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate cancer, and gastric cancer, they hypothesized its predictive role in DLBCL and conducted further verification. This method reduces the exploration time of tumor biomarkers and has become the preferred choice for many researchers. However, its specificity and sensitivity fail to achieve satisfactory results. Another method is to develop a prognostic prediction model by selecting meaningful laboratory and imaging indicators based on extensive studies of patients with DLBCL. Among them, the most widely used one is the IPI system. Nevertheless, in light of advancements in detection methods and shifts in treatment approaches, an increasing number of researchers have endeavored to further enrich and modify the IPI in recent years. A single-center retrospective study in the United Kingdom examined the relationship between diagnostic waiting time (DWT), defined as the interval from the initial consultation to diagnosis, and the IPI in patients with DLBCL, analyzing its impact on survival rates. The study ultimately found that longer DWT was associated with poorer prognosis. The NCCN-IPI is an enhanced version of the IPI, proposed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), with the aim of improving the accuracy of prognostic prediction. Building upon the factors considered in the IPI, the NCCN-IPI incorporates the results of immunophenotyping (such as BCL2, BCL6, MYC, etc.) and other clinical characteristics, thereby forming a more sophisticated scoring system. This refined model has been demonstrated to possess superior predictive accuracy. In recent years, numerous high-throughput sequencing methods, including metabolomics sequencing, have been widely applied to the diagnosis and prognosis modeling of diseases, providing novel insights into the development of predictive models. The significant role of amino acid metabolism in cancer has also been widely reported. Inspired by researchers' efforts to improve the IPI prognostic system, and integrating the latest findings in metabolomics, we have achieved a synthesis of these two approaches. In this study, the plasma samples of DLBCL patients and healthy controls were studied via targeted metabolomics, the amino acids in the samples were quantitatively detected, and the data were analyzed via cluster analysis. Combined with the clinical prognosis data of patients, the amino acid metabolism profile of DLBCL was established, and potential biomarkers of DLBCL were screened to assist early clinical diagnosis and prognostic analysis of DLBCL. Metabolic pathway analysis was also performed to explore more potential information related to disease progression.
Differential expression of amino acids in DLBCL

Growing evidence indicates that reprogramming amino acid metabolism is crucial for meeting the heightened nutritional demands for energy and biosynthesis in lymphoma proliferation. For instance, lymphoma cells require substantial amounts of glutamine:essential for lymphocyte activation:as the body utilizes it for energy production, macromolecule synthesis, redox homeostasis, and oxidative stress resistance. We hypothesized that such high energy consumption might be associated with the overexpression of amino acids to provide energy pathways for the hypermetabolism of tumor cells. In this study, we found that 8 amino acids were indeed abnormally expressed in DLBCL patients, among which Asp, Glu, Phe, and Thr were overexpressed in DLBCL. The expression of Gly, His, Ser, and Trp in DLBCL patients was lower than that in normal controls.

The abnormal expression of a variety of amino acids in DLBCL patients suggests that amino acid metabolism is disrupted in patients with lymphoma. We reviewed the literature related to amino acid metabolism in DLBCL and found that there is an earlier study on the metabolic abnormalities associated with glutamine breakdown in DLBCL. Glutamine metabolism plays an important role in the process of lymphocyte proliferation. According to our targeted metabolomics analysis, glutamate is upregulated in the plasma of DLBCL patients, and glutamate easily forms glutamine with blood ammonia after it is absorbed by the body.
Amino acids and the prognosis of DLBCL patients

DLBCL is a complex entity with varied clinical presentations, genetic outcomes, therapeutic responses, and prognoses. Next-generation sequencing of DLBCL has enabled the identification of diverse genetic abnormalities, revealing that GCB and ABC tumors exhibit distinct mutation profiles. However, owing to the variability of mutated genes and the complexity and cost of genetic testing, identifying genetic abnormalities in these tumors is difficult. It is not yet possible for every genetic test to be routinely used in clinical practice. To identify potential biomarkers that can predict the prognosis of patients, we aimed to clarify whether amino acid differences are associated with patient prognosis. The sPLS-DA model was established to screen two amino acids, glutamine and tryptophan, that are significantly associated with the clinical prognosis of patients via bioinformatics analysis. It has been confirmed that glutamine can affect the occurrence and development of DLBCL, suggesting that amino acids, as potential DLBCL biomarkers, may help us predict the disease in advance to assist early clinical diagnosis and prognosis analysis. In addition, with respect to the effects of tryptophan and glutamine on the prognosis of DLBCL patients, many future studies are needed to discover additional potential mechanisms. Ultimately, as a new biomarker for the diagnosis and prognosis prediction of DLBCL, our results encourage scholars to study the mechanism of abnormal amino acid expression and lay a solid foundation for better management of DLBCL and drug development.
Amino acid metabolic pathways associated with DLBCL prognosis
D-Gln and D-Glu metabolism

Our study revealed that the D-Gln and D-Glu metabolic pathway is related to the prognosis of DLBCL patients. We speculate that this pathway may affect the prognosis of DLBCL by affecting the energy metabolism and growth of tumor cells, since one pathway of D-Gln catabolism is the conversion of D-Gln to D-Glu (e.g., glutaminase). In genetic and biochemical studies of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the DguA protein was shown to be a D-amino acid dehydrogenase. The D-Glu formed by the decomposition of D-Gln can be deaminated by DguA oxidation. These results identify the oxidative deamination of DguA as a fundamental pathway for D-Glu catabolism. Deamination of D-Glu by DguA results in the generation of alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia, which can be used as carbon and nitrogen sources through the tricarboxylic acid cycle and ammonia assimilation pathway, respectively, thus providing energy support to tumor cells. DguA can also promote susceptibility to mutations induced by benzene metabolites by upregulating the Bcl-2 protein, which is a novel mechanism of benzene carcinogenesis. In addition, some studies have shown that D-Gln and D-Glu metabolism are related to poor prognosis in prostate cancer patients. The role of metabolic reprogramming in cancer has been extensively explored. The expression of Glutaminase-1 (GLS1) can be strongly detected in both DLBCL biopsy samples and cell lines. Regardless of the subtype classification of DLBCL cells, pharmacological inhibition and gene knockdown of GLS1 can induce cell death, while primary B cells remain unaffected. D-Gln catabolism plays a crucial role in resisting oxidative stress, and targeting GLS1 may be a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with DLBCL. DLBCL consume mitochondrial pyruvate via glutamate-pyruvate transaminase 2 to enable alpha-ketoglutarate (alpha-KG) production as part of glutaminolysis. That is to say, mitochondrial pyruvate supports the proliferation of lymphoma by promoting the glutaminolysis pathway dependent on glutamate pyruvate transaminase 2. Additionally, a research demonstrated that administering DM-alphaKG, a cell-permeable form of alpha-KG, markedly inhibited tumor progression by triggering both apoptotic and non-apoptotic cell death mechanisms. The buildup of alpha-KG enhanced oxidative stress in double-hit lymphoma, a process mediated by the conversion of 2-hydroxyglutarate through malate dehydrogenase 1. Elevated reactive oxygen species levels played a crucial role in inducing ferroptosis by facilitating lipid peroxidation and activating TP53. In conclusion, the mechanisms by which the D-Gln and D-Glu metabolic pathways affect DLBCL are complex and diverse, and more in - depth and extensive exploration should be carried out.
Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis

Aromatic amino acids, including Trp, Tyr, and Phe, are key precursors for monoaminergic neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, which are essential for various physiological processes, particularly in regulating behavior and emotions. These amino acids also play crucial roles in tumor metabolism. Tryptophan and phenylalanine, which are dietary essentials, contribute to serotonin production and the synthesis of tyrosine, respectively. The conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, catalyzed by the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, primarily occurs in the liver but also in other tissues, including the kidney, pancreas, and brain. Studies suggest that inflammation or malignancy can alter phenylalanine hydroxylase activity. Research on untreated DLBCL patients' gut microbiota indicates that phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis functions are disrupted, regardless of pathology or gastrointestinal involvement. Generally, tyrosine metabolism is downregulated in DLBCL, and these metabolic disruptions may contribute to oncogenesis and vary across lymphoma types. A recent study has confirmed that Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors can block B - cell receptor signaling and are particularly effective against specific subtypes of DLBCL such as MCD. BTK inhibitors promote the autophagic degradation of MYD88L265P, which may be the reason for the therapeutic efficacy. Metabolites of tryptophan metabolism in the tumor microenvironment play a crucial immunosuppressive role in various cancers. Recent studies have also confirmed a close relationship between tryptophan metabolism and DLBCL. The rate-limiting enzyme in tryptophan catabolism, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), is essential for the proliferation of DLBCL cells and may represent a potential therapeutic target for DLBCL. Additionally, lower levels of phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan have been reported in the body fluids and tissues of patients with malignant esophageal and gastric cancers. Our study emphasizes the significance of the phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis pathways in DLBCL prognosis, though further research is needed to clarify their roles and mechanisms.
Alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism

The alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolic pathways are characteristic of pathological metabolic disorders in diabetes, and have also been implicated in ischemic stroke research. In studies on human neuroblastoma, the neurotoxic amino acid BMAA disrupts these pathways in neuron-like cells. In antibiotic resistance research, these pathways are inactive. Our findings suggest that alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism may contribute to the poor prognosis of DLBCL patients. However, we found limited literature connecting this pathway to DLBCL, indicating a gap in research on its role in DLBCL prognosis.
Establishment of prognostic models based on key amino acids and clinical data

PLSR extracts essential features from nonlinearly transformed variables and identifies key variables from the original input variables, eliminating correlations among all independent variables and establishing an optimal model to link these variables with the target outputs. Consequently, PLSR has been applied in the construction of prognostic models to increase prediction accuracy and reliability. To further validate the reliability of the established prognostic models with relevant data, an SVR machine learning model was applied. SVR is a sophisticated machine learning model distinct from PLSR, processing nonlinear data through kernel functions. The radial basis kernel function was employed, enhancing the ability to capture complex data patterns. Additionally, the robustness of SVR makes it well suited for real-world research with noise. SVR can be trained with small samples while maintaining good generalization performance. After the outcomes of these two modeling methods were compared, the feasibility of incorporating key amino acids and critical clinical data into the PFS prognostic model was demonstrated, as was the close correlation between aberrantly expressed amino acids and patient prognosis.

This study advances DLBCL prognosis research through two key innovations: the integration of targeted metabolomics with clinical parameters to identify potential biomarkers, and the first comprehensive characterization of amino acid metabolic dysregulation in DLBCL, revealing actionable therapeutic targets. Our hybrid analytical approach (PLSR-SVR modeling) significantly enhances prognostic precision by correlating metabolic profiles with clinical outcomes. The retrospective single-center design precludes causal inferences, and the moderate sample size (n = 20) may underrepresent DLBCL's molecular heterogeneity. While metabolomic profiling provides mechanistic insights, larger multicenter validations are needed to establish clinical utility. These findings position amino acid metabolism as a promising prognostic axis in DLBCL, warranting mechanistic studies and prospective trials to translate metabolic biomarkers into personalized management strategies.
Conclusion

In conclusion, this study successfully developed a plasma amino acid metabolic profile model to differentiate DLBCL patients from healthy controls using the LC-MS/MS technique. The analysis revealed abnormal plasma amino acid expression in DLBCL patients, and bioinformatics analysis confirmed that these abnormalities were significantly associated with patient prognosis. Our findings identified statistically significant differential amino acids in plasma, specifically Asp, Glu, Phe, Thr, Gly, His, Ser, and Trp, with tryptophan and glutamine showing significant correlations with prognosis. Additionally, three amino acid pathways potentially influencing patient prognosis were identified: D-Gln and D-Glu metabolism, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis, and alanine, aspartic acid, and glutamate metabolism. These findings suggest that plasma amino acids may be used as indicators of disease prognosis, but the specific mechanisms must be further researched and verified. This study provides a strong basis for the use of amino acids as a clinical screening tool for the diagnosis and prognosis of DLBCL, suggesting that finding specific biomarkers from the plasma amino acid metabolic profile has great prospects for applications in the detection of DLBCL and provides a new research direction for the diagnosis and treatment of DLBCL. We have developed two prognostic models based on tryptophan, glutamine, and key clinical data, providing an example for the integration of biomedical research and DLBCL.

passages.text: In situ NMR reveals a pH sensor motif in an outer membrane protein that drives bacterial vesicle production
Significance

The Salmonella surface protein PagC is a major driver of extracellular vesicle formation. Here, we show that this phenotype is transferrable to Escherichia coli, another diderm, Gram-negative bacterium. PagC increases vesicle production in E. coli. Three histidines, essential for vesiculation, become protonated at acidic pH, and acidic pH promotes aggregation of bacterial cells and outer membrane vesicles (OMVs). NMR of PagC in native vesicles is introduced as an important tool for in situ structural analysis of bacterial membrane proteins. The results have important implications for understanding the factors that drive the bacterial extracellular vesicle secretion, as well as their roles as vaccine, drug delivery, and nanotechnology platforms.

The outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) produced by diderm bacteria have important roles in cell envelope homeostasis, secretion, interbacterial communication, and pathogenesis. The facultative intracellular pathogen Salmonella enterica Typhimurium (STm) activates OMV biogenesis inside the acidic vacuoles of host cells by upregulating the expression of the OM protein PagC, one of the most robustly activated genes in a host environment. Here, we used solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and electron microscopy (EM), with native bacterial OMVs, to demonstrate that three histidines, essential for the OMV biogenic function of PagC, constitute a key pH-sensing motif. The NMR spectra of PagC in OMVs show that they become protonated around pH 6, and His protonation is associated with specific perturbations of select regions of PagC. The use of bacterial OMVs is a key aspect of this work enabling NMR structural studies in the context of the physiological environment. PagC expression upregulates OMV production in Escherichia coli, replicating its function in STm. Moreover, the presence of PagC drives a striking aggregation of OMVs and increases bacterial cell pellicle formation at acidic pH, pointing to a potential role as an adhesin active in biofilm formation. The data provide experimental evidence for a pH-dependent mechanism of OMV biogenesis and aggregation driven by an OM protein.

Extracellular vesicle secretion is a fundamental membrane remodeling process shared by eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells across all kingdoms of life. In diderm bacteria, including Gram-negative species, the vesicles released from the outer membrane (OM) perform many functions important for host infection, environmental adaptation, and colonization and also have important roles as vaccine, drug delivery, and nanotechnology platforms. While curvature-inducing proteins are known to play prominent roles in actively driving eukaryotic membrane remodeling and vesiculation by scaffolding or wedging, the mechanisms governing prokaryotic membrane curvature and OM vesicle (OMV) biogenesis are not well understood and generally thought to be more passive processes driven by disruption of OM-peptidoglycan connections, periplasmic accumulation of misfolded biomolecules, or incorporation of modified LPS in the outer leaflet of the OM. In this study, we present evidence that the OM protein PagC, which promotes OM vesiculation in Salmonella, acts as a pH sensor and active driver of OMV biogenesis and can confer this phenotype to another Gram-negative bacterium, Escherichia coli.

In Salmonella, PagC expression is induced by the PhoPQ regulon upon exposure to acidic pH, divalent cation limitation, or cationic antimicrobial peptides. Notably, PagC is sufficient for promoting OMV production by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm), even in the absence of LPS-modifying enzymes. The vesiculation activity is largely localized to two sequences harboring three histidines (H60, H62, and H102) in the second and third extracellular loops (EL2 and EL3) of its predicted eight-stranded beta-barrel structure (Fig. 1 and SI Appendix, Fig. S1). This locus is an attractive candidate for a pH-sensing motif because the typical acid dissociation constant (pKa~6) of His sidechains makes them susceptible to protonation and positive charge acquisition in the acidic intravacuolar environment encountered by STm during infection.

Structural model of PagC. (A) Representative structure of PagC, taken at 2,998 ns of MD simulation in the OM, showing the three His and two Phe side chains (yellow sticks) in the proposed pH-sensing motif. The OM includes LPS (blue, green, and pink lines) and phospholipid (yellow lines). (B) Inverse sequence alignment of the ascending and descending neighboring segments of EL2 and EL3. Alignments are rendered with ClustalX coloring.

Given that acidic pH is one of the most potent activating signals for the PhoPQ regulon, the subset of activated genes, including PagC, may be expected to respond to environmental pH. Indeed, mimicking acidic conditions by mutating His to positively charged Lys generates a superactivated PagC mutant that overproduces OMVs compared to wild-type, while mutations to Ala dramatically suppress OMV production. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations suggest that PagC can alter its shape and dynamics from a cylinder at neutral pH, to a wedge at acidic pH. This could induce OM curvature and vesiculation, but whether the PagC histidines are susceptible to protonation, and whether PagC undergoes conformational change, have remained open questions.

Here, we used solid-state NMR and electron microscopy (EM), with PagC in E. coli bacterial OMVs, to analyze the effects of pH on His protonation, PagC conformation, and OMV structure. The data show that H60, H62, and H102 become protonated at acidic pH, and acidic pH induces specific changes in select regions of the protein. PagC expression appears to promote OMV production in E. coli, replicating its function in STm and reinforcing its role as a unique active driver of OMV biogenesis. Moreover, acidic pH induces extensive OMV autoaggregation and bacterial cell pellicle formation, suggesting a potential role of PagC in biofilm formation. The data point to an active mechanism for pH-dependent modulation of OMV biogenesis by a bacterial OM protein.
Results and Discussion
PagC Localizes to E. coli OMVs.

Bacterial OMVs have the same membrane organization as the parental bacterial OM, including an inner leaflet composed of phospholipids, an outer leaflet composed of LPS, and various OM proteins (Fig. 1A). This highly asymmetric membrane organization is essential for supporting protein structure and function yet not easily mimicked in samples reconstituted from purified components. To analyze the structure and activity of PagC in the native context, we sought to work with native OMVs isolated from bacteria modified only by an inducible pagC gene. Since E. coli has been shown to support activities of PagC, we transformed Lemo21(DE3) E. coli cells with a pagC-encoding, IPTG-inducible plasmid and isolated OMVs from the culture media for analysis.

SDS-PAGE and western blots (Fig. 2A) show that the resulting OMVs are enriched in plasmid-encoded PagC (pPagC) relative to whole cells, as reported for STm. The appearance of a heat-modifiable band that shifts from ~14 kDa to 18 kDa upon heat denaturation demonstrates that the protein is folded and behaves as an integral membrane beta-barrel. OMVs isolated from cells transformed with empty plasmid vector (pEV), but otherwise cultured and induced as pPagC cells, do not contain PagC and therefore serve as a valuable negative control. As a further control, we isolated OMVs from cells expressing plasmid-encoded Ail (pAil), the PagC homolog from the pathogen Yersinia pestis. Like PagC, Ail localizes to both the E. coli cell OM and secreted OMVs and displays the characteristic heat modifiability of OM beta-barrels (Fig. 2B).

PagC expressed in E. coli localizes to OMVs. (A and B) SDS-PAGE of whole cells and OMVs isolated from pPagC, pEV (empty plasmid), or pAil bacteria. Proteins were visualized with Coomassie stain (Top) or immunoblotting with PagC-specific antibody (alpha-PacC, Bottom). Arrows mark bands from folded (F) and heat-unfolded (U) proteins. (C-G) Representative cryo-EM (C and D) or negative stain EM (E-G) of pPagC, pEV, and pAil OMVs at pH 7. (H) OMV size estimates from negative stain EM analysis. For each of pPagC, pEV, or pAil E. coli, 500 OMVs were selected for analysis using FIJI. Statistical significance (n >= 3 biological replicates) was calculated using unpaired Student's two-tailed test and set at a P value < 0.05 (****P < 0.0001). (I) Measurement of light absorbance at 400 and 280 nm for pPagC, pEV, or pAil E. coli. A280 measurements were corrected for light scattering at 380 and 400 nm. Bars represent mean values and error bars SEM (seven biological replicates).

All three OMV types (pPagC, pEV, and pAil) are highly enriched in the major porin OmpF, as evidenced by SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry. OmpF facilitates the general passive diffusion of polar molecules (600 to 700 Da) across the OM and is a known component of the OMV proteome where it supports the exchange of solutes and protects vesicle structures from osmotic stress. Interestingly, SDS-PAGE densitometry indicates that while Ail resides primarily in the cellular OM (Ail/OmpF = 26/74 in OMVs), PagC is preferentially enriched in OMVs (PagC/OmpF = 68/32 in OMVs). The localization of PagC to E. coli OMVs is in line with its reported behavior in STm and points to a specific property that distinguishes it from its homolog Ail.

Cryogenic EM shows that both pPagC and pEV OMVs adopt discrete spherical structures (Fig. 2 C and D), with a distinct single membrane and the two leaflets of the lipid bilayer clearly resolved in electron-dense regions, as described for OMVs from other diderm bacteria. Moreover, negative stain EM shows that pPagC, pEV, and pAil OMVs each have relatively uniform size (Fig. 2 E-G), but PagC expression increases the average OMV diameter to 41.3 nm compared to the averages of 34.2 and 35 nm observed for pEV and pAil OMVs (Fig. 2H). The results are in line with size estimates of STm OMVs in the 20 to 40 nm range based on transmission EM but differ from the larger (~165 nm) diameter estimates based on nanoparticle tracking analysis. Alphas noted previously, these differences reflect the experimental sizing approaches: Nanoparticle tracking, commonly used in extracellular vesicle studies, fails to report vesicle diameters below 60 nm, while an important advantage of EM is the ability to select only biogenic OMVs and exclude the typically larger and often multilamellar vesicular structures that can result from explosive cell lysis (SI Appendix, Fig. S2). Thus, we conclude that biogenic OMVs of similar shape and size are observed in engineered E. coli as in STm.

Finally, PagC expression appears to result in approximately twofold higher yield of OMVs compared to either pEV or pAil, as estimated by both light scattering and UV absorbance (Fig. 2I). The data therefore indicate that the vesiculation activity of PagC observed in STm is also reproduced in E. coli, and provide further evidence that OMV activation is a PagC-specific property.
Solid-State NMR Analysis of PagC OMVs.

Solid-state NMR is ideally suited for structural studies of integral membrane proteins in lipid assemblies, including bacterial cell envelopes and membranes. Here, we took biogenic OMVs isolated from E. coli directly for solid-state NMR analysis. To achieve PagC-targeted 15N and 13C isotope labeling, and suppress NMR signals arising from endogenous E. coli proteins, we used a protocol where the T7/DE3-mediated expression of plasmid-encoded PagC is coupled with the suppression of chromosomal gene transcription by the antibiotic rifampicin. The cells were first grown in unlabeled minimal media and only transferred to isotopically labeled media to induce protein expression. OMVs were isolated from the culture media and packed into 3.2 mm magic angle spinning (MAS) rotors for NMR experiments.

The 15N and 13C spectra of pPagC OMVs (Fig. 3, black), obtained with 1H-15N, 1H-13C, and 1H-15N-13C cross-polarization (CP), contain signals from protein, as well as lipid and LPS acyl chains, glycans, aminoglycans and potentially peptidoglycan. These cellular building blocks continue to be produced and incorporate 13C and 15N during the isotope labeling period of cell culture and are known components of the bacterial OMV lumen. Their NMR signals have been observed in the spectra of cell envelope samples and may be assigned by comparison.

NMR spectra of PagC in E. coli OMVs. Spectra were acquired at 4  C for pPagC (black) or pEV (blue) OMVs at pH 7. (A-C) One-dimensional spectra acquired with 1H-15N CP (A), 1H-13C CP (B), or 1H-15N followed by 15N-13C CP (C). Signals from protein and LPS sites are marked (LPS GN: glucosamine). (D) Two-dimensional 13C/13C correlation PDSD spectra. Assignments to residue types are marked in Inset boxes.

By contrast, little evidence of protein NMR signals is seen in the spectra of pEV OMVs, isolated from cells transformed with empty plasmid vector, but otherwise grown and induced in an identical manner as pPagC cells (Fig. 3, blue). The 13C spectrum obtained by 1H-13C CP has both greater lipid signal intensity at 33 ppm (~30%), as well as much lower protein signal at 54 ppm (~60%) and 19 ppm (100%), for pEV versus pPagC OMVs (Fig. 3B), and the 13C spectrum obtained by 1H-15N-13C polarization transfer shows a dramatic signal reduction (Fig. 3C).

The two-dimensional 13C/13C correlation spectrum of pPagC OMVs (Fig. 3D, black) has many resolved signals from Ala, Ile, Pro, Ser, and Thr spin systems. These can be easily identified based on their characteristic chemical shifts at positions consistent with beta-strand structure. By contrast, the spectrum of pEV OMVs (Fig. 3D, blue) has no detectable signals from protein, confirming that the expression system leads to highly selective isotope labeling of the target with minimal background, notwithstanding the abundance of OmpF and other proteins in the OMVs.
The Histidines of PagC Are Sensitive to pH.

The proposed pH sensing motif of PagC comprises two inverse homology sequences (Fig. 1 and SI Appendix, Fig. S1) each located in the descending segment of EL2 (residues 62 to 69) and ascending segment of EL3 (residues 95 to 102). MD simulations revealed a role for these sites in forming a series of EL2-EL3 cross contacts, including H60/H62-H102 and F65-F99 ring stacking, that stabilize the loop conformations and couple their dynamics. By contrast, protonated His generate electrostatic repulsions that decouple EL2 and EL3, altering both the conformation of PagC and its interactions with OM lipids and LPS. This model aligns with the known low pH activation of PagC and the His mutagenesis data, but neither His protonation in the bacterial OM nor the existence of an EL2-EL3 pH sensing motif that can switch conformation upon transfer to acidic environments, has been explored experimentally.

To address the question of His protonation, we acquired 15N NMR spectra for a series of pPagC OMVs incubated in buffers ranging from pH 8.5 to pH 4 (Fig. 4A). The 15N chemical shift tensors of His imidazole Nd and Ne nitrogens are well characterized, and isotropic 15N chemical shifts are good indicators of both His protonation and hydrogen bonding. Environmental pH has a dramatic effect on the 15N spectra of the His imidazole nitrogens of PagC. At pH 8.5, a broad envelope of signal intensity is observed between 172 and 260 ppm. Based on reported values of His 15N chemical shifts, the 172 to 182 ppm intensity may be assigned to protonated Ne and Nd, while the weak 245 to 260 ppm signal likely reflects deprotonated nitrogens which are more challenging to detect by 1H-15N CP due to the lack of bound hydrogen. Overall, the absence of resolved peaks, combined with the weak broad signal intensity near 207 ppm, reflect a mix of neutral tautomeric states with either Nd (tau tautomer) or Ne (pi tautomer) protonation, exchanging slower than the mus timescale of the 15N NMR experiment (Fig. 4B).

pH titration of PagC His. (A) One-dimensional 15N spectra of pPagC OMVs acquired at 4  C with 1H-15N CP at pH 4 (8,000 scans), pH 5 (30,000 scans), pH 6 (86,000 scans); pH 7 (117,000 scans); and pH 8 (160,000 scans). The spectra were processed with a shifted sine bell function (SSB = 3) for pH 4 to 6, or exponential line broadening functions for pH 7 (LB = 50) and pH 8.5 (LB = 100). Dashed lines align with resolved signals. (B) Structures of the tautomeric states of the neutral His imidazole ring and fully protonated imidazolium cation.

As the pH is lowered, the 207 ppm intensity disappears, and resolved spectral components between ~172 and 181 ppm grow in intensity with progressive line narrowing. Three signals resolved at pH 6, and four resolved at pH 5 and pH 4, may be assigned to protonated Ne and Nd of the imidazolium cation. The signal observed at 180.1 (pH 4) and 181.1 ppm (pH 6 and pH 5) is consistent with hydrogen bonding of a protonated imidazole nitrogen to a carboxylate group.

The spectra are complex. The observation of three to four 15N signals for three His may reflect rapid imidazole ring rotations that average the two chemically inequivalent Ne and Nd sites of each His, spectral overlap of distinct Ne and Nd signals, or selective detection of specific His residues with favorable hydrogen bonding or dynamics for NMR observation by CP. Absent resonance assignment, it is impossible to distinguish among these mechanisms, but the data unequivocally demonstrate that the His of PagC are water-accessible and sensitive to environmental pH and protonation near pH 6.
Effect of pH on the Conformation of PagC.

To probe the effect of pH on other protein sites, we acquired 15N/13C and 13C/13C correlation spectra of pPagC OMVs exposed to either pH 7 or pH 4 buffer (Fig. 5 A and B and SI Appendix, Figs. S3 and S4). Both 15N/13C and 13C/13C spectra compare favorably with those of the PagC homolog Ail in the bacterial cell envelope, demonstrating the potential of NMR characterization of membrane proteins in biogenic OMVs. The NMR signal intensity is ~50% greater at pH 4 than pH 7, and the number of scans was adjusted to compensate for this difference (SI Appendix, Table S1), which likely arises from a strong OMV aggregation effect observed at pH 4 (see below) allowing us to pack more sample into the rotor, and potentially some enhancement of 1H-13C CP due to increased protonation of exchangeable sites.

Effect of pH on the 15N/13C and 13C/13C NMR spectra of PagC in E. coli OMVs. Spectra were acquired at 4  C for pPagC OMVs at pH 7 (black) or pH 4 (red). (A) Two-dimensional 15N/13C TEDOR NCA spectra. (B) Two-dimensional 13C/13C PDSD spectral regions selected to show signals from Pro, Ala, Thr, and Ile. (C and D) Structural models taken from MD simulations of His-neutral (C; 2,998 ns) or His-protonated (D; 2,668 ns) PagC, showing His and Phe sidechains (yellow stick), and CA atoms (sphere) of Ala (yellow), Ile (wheat), Pro (red), and Thr (green). The OM includes LPS (blue, green, and pink lines) and phospholipid (PL: yellow lines).

The 15N/13C spectra acquired with transfer echo double resonance (TEDOR) mixing have excellent signal intensity and resolution, with line widths of well-resolved signals in the range of 0.6 to 0.8 ppm for 13C, and 1.3 to 1.8 ppm for 15N (SI Appendix, Fig. S3). Many signals can be resolved from the eighteen Gly, four Pro, six Thr, nine Ala, and seven Ile in the sequence, including Pro N-Ca and N-Cd correlations. Since these residues are distributed across the length of the PagC beta-barrel their NMR signals are valuable probes of protein conformation (Fig. 5 C and D).

The 15N and 13C chemical shifts from these sites reflect beta-stranded secondary structure, and the spectra obtained at pH 7 and pH 4 display extensive signal overlap, indicating that the overall conformation of PagC is maintained irrespective of pH. Notably, there are also several 15N and 13C chemical shift perturbations of select signals. For example, two Thr (T98 and T104) are located in EL3 and two Thr signals are perturbed by pH in the 13C/13C spectrum (Fig. 5B and SI Appendix, Fig. S4). Moreover, select signals from hydrophobic Ala and Ile, and at least two of the Pro Ca-Cd signals, are perturbed in response to pH. While the lack of resonance assignments precludes a detailed spectral analysis, such selective peak perturbation reflects a site-specific response to the local environment of neighboring protein and LPS moieties, rather than a wholesale effect of buffer pH. Structure determination will be needed to determine the specific conformational change elicited by pH.
PagC Induces OMV Autoaggregation and Pellicle Formation at Acidic pH.

In the process of NMR sample preparation, we noticed a marked flocculation of pPagC OMVs occurring immediately upon transfer to pH 4, and this prompted us to examine the ultrastructural impact of pH. Negative stain EM of freshly prepared OMVs reveals striking aggregation of pPagC but not pEV OMVs at acidic pH (Fig. 6A and SI Appendix, Fig. S5). While all OMVs are well dispersed at pH 7.5, pPagC OMVs lightly cluster at pH 6, and the dominant features at pH 5 and pH 4 are extensive aggregates with clear evidence of membrane fusion and some structures resembling wire-like OMV connections (Fig. 6A, arrow) similar to those described for Myxococcus xanthus. Although we could identify some solitary nonaggregated vesicles, their abundance was substantially reduced relative to neutral pH. Aggregation appears to initiate around pH 6 and complete fusion is observed at pH 4.

PagC induces pH-dependent OMV aggregation and bacterial cell pellicle formation. (A and B) Representative negative stain EM of pPagC (Top) and pEV (Bottom) OMVs, acquired at pH 7.5, pH 6, pH 5, pH 4 (A) or pH 7.5 after incubation at pH 4 (B). The white arrow points to a wire-like OMV connection at pH5. (C) Pellicle formation by pPagC, pEV, and pAil E. coli cells. Cells were suspended in 2 mL of M9 minimal media (OD600 = 0.5) in 15 x 100 mm glass tubes and incubated for 16 h at 37  C. After removing the cells by centrifugation, the interior glass walls were treated with methanol and air dried overnight, then washed three times with buffer, treated with 2.5 mL of crystal violet solution (0.1% for 10 min), then washed with buffer, and air dried. Pellicle formation was detected as a violet-stained rim at the air-water interface.

To test the reversibility of this phenomenon, we performed EM on pPagC OMVs incubated first at pH 4 overnight and then switched to pH 7.5 for another 12 h (Fig. 6B and SI Appendix, Fig. S5). Although many aggregate masses remain, some are visibly dissolved, suggesting some degree of reversibility. Tightly associated OMVs appear to form a mosaic-like structure in which the vesicle membranes flatten against each other increasing the contact surface. Moreover, some membranes appear to have fused, suggesting not only that PagC promotes aggregation but also that it may mediate membrane fusion.

Finally, we tested the ability of PagC to induce E. coli cell pellicle formation at pH 7.6 and pH 5.8 where its OMV-producing activity in STm is documented. At pH 7.6 there is minimal evidence of pellicle formation at the air-water interface, but a substantial pellicle forms at pH 5.8 as readily visualized by staining with crystal violet (Fig. 6C and SI Appendix, Fig. S6). By contrast, pEV cells form very little pellicle at either neutral or acidic pH, while pAil cells produce dense pellicles regardless of pH, in line with the documented aggregation activity of Ail in both its native Y. pestis and E. coli.

These results align with the reported association of PagC with biofilm formation and multiple drug resistance in S. enterica as well as growing evidence that OMVs are common constituents of the microbial biofilm extracellular matrix and play an active role in biofilm formation. The pH-dependent reversible aggregation may reflect a mechanism for environmental adaptation whereby secreted OMVs aggregate to form an adhesive matrix at low pH, that can be quickly undone upon transfer to a neutral pH environment. Such a process could be important for the survival of Salmonella in environments of extreme pH fluctuation, such as the human digestive tract. The aggregation phenotypes remain to be demonstrated in Salmonella. Nontyphoidal Salmonella produce an alternative group IV O-antigen capsule that is implicated in environmental survival, immune evasion, and biofilm formation, while the LPS core of E. coli B strains, including Lemo21(DE3) used in this study, lacks O-antigen repeats and capsular biosynthesis and thus may artificially unmask PagC exposing its loops to the OMV surface and activating aggregation.
Conclusions

OMV secretion is a major membrane remodeling process essential for bacterial colony behavior and environmental adaptation. Recently, we proposed that His protonation drives a conformational change of PagC from an ordered cylindrical barrel to a wedge, where EL2 and EL3 are decoupled and exert pressure on the outer leaflet of the OM, resulting in curvature and vesicle budding. Here, we have shown that the histidines of PagC are indeed pH-sensitive and their protonation is associated with perturbations of specific PagC sites. The NMR spectra show that PagC adopts an overall beta-stranded conformation in bacterial OMVs and the His sidechains titrate from neutral tautomeric states to the protonated imidazolium cation near pH 6. Whether Asp and Glu residues in the extracellular loops are also susceptible to protonation and contribute to conformational change is an interesting question that should be addressed in future studies. Overall, the NMR data reflect a specific response of PagC to environmental pH and provide experimental support for an active role as a pH sensor and driver of OM curvature.

The use of bacterial OMVs is an essential aspect of our study enabling structural analysis in the context of the native environment. Working with native samples is particularly important for bacterial OM proteins, which have coevolved with LPS to confer species-specific properties and function as a coordinated assembly with the highly asymmetric environment of the OM. Here, the OMV-producing activity of PagC observed in STm was recapitulated in a B strain E. coli derivative, and the propensity of PagC to promote OMV aggregation and bacterial pellicle formation at low pH was identified as a potentially important property of this protein. With the caveat that the R1 type LPS of our B strain E. coli may unmask the PagC aggregation phenotype, this finding aligns with evidence for the association of PagC with biofilm formation and multiple drug resistance in S. enterica.

OMVs isolated from engineered E. coli have been proposed as an in situ platform for solution NMR studies of periplasmic proteins or periplasmic domains of membrane proteins. This application, however, relied on the deletion of multiple OM protein genes and vesicle size homogenization by filtered extrusion. Moreover, the use of solution NMR excludes the possibility of examining integral membrane proteins whose dynamics are coupled to the relatively immobile OMV structure. Here, we took native E. coli OMVs with the full complement of endogenous, chromosomally encoded OM proteins, directly for solid-state NMR analysis. This work, therefore, paves the way for NMR studies of physiological bacterial OMVs, including those produced by Salmonella and other pathogens.

In conclusion, this study provides experimental evidence for the role of PagC as an active pH sensor and a driver of OMV biogenesis, it describes a potential role of PagC as a regulator of OMV aggregation and pellicle formation, and introduces OMVs as an important platform for in situ NMR structural analysis of OM proteins.
Materials and Methods
Bacterial Strains, Culture Conditions, and Key Reagents.

All E. coli were commercially available Lemo21(DE3) (New England BioLabs, MA). The pET22b(+)-pagC plasmid (pPagC) for IPTG-inducible expression of PagC lacking the endogenous signal peptide was designed in-frame with the PelB signal peptide and acquired from Genscript (Piscataway, NJ). The Empty vector bacteria were transformed with empty pET22b(+) plasmid (pEV). The plasmid for IPTG-inducible expression of Ail (pAil) was described previously. Western blots were performed with a custom (Thermo Fisher Scientific, IL) polyclonal antibody against the PagC EL3 peptide CDGDSFSNKISSRKTGFAWG. Bacteria were cultured in M9 media supplemented with 0.2% glucose, 100 microg/mL ampicillin, and 35 microg/mL chloramphenicol when appropriate. SDS-PAGE band densitometry was analyzed using VisionWorks 4+ (Analytik Jena), Fiji Image J, and Adobe Photoshop, and the average value taken.
Isotope Labeling of PagC.

Transformed bacteria (pPagC, pEV, and pAil) were grown overnight at 37  C in unlabeled M9 media. Overnight cultures were used to inoculate fresh unlabeled M9 to achieve OD600 = 0.1 and cells were incubated with shaking at 37  C. At OD600 = 0.6, expression of the DE3 RNA polymerase was induced by adding 0.4 mM IPTG. Following a 10-min incubation, the cells were pelleted (5,000 x g, 4  C, 20 min) and resuspended in M9 supplemented with 1 g/L of 15N ammonium sulfate and 0.2% 13C glucose (Cambridge Isotope Laboratories, MA), IPTG and rifampicin were added to 0.4 mM and 100 microg/mL, respectively, and expression was allowed to proceed for 16 h at 26  C prior to harvesting.
OMV Isolation and Characterization.

OMVs were harvested by diafiltration and ultracentrifugation. The cultures were centrifuged (5,000 x g, 4  C, 20 min) to remove bacterial cells, and the resulting supernatants were centrifuged again to remove residual bacteria. This supernatant was passed through a 0.45 microm filter to remove residual bacteria and large aggregates, and the filtrate was concentrated using an Amicon stirred cell fitted with a 300 kDa PES membrane disc filter (Millipore Sigma, St. Louis, MO). OMVs in the concentrated filtrates were harvested by centrifugation (150,000 x g, 4  C, 1.5 h), and resuspended in buffer for analysis. All OMV buffers contained 0.9 mM CaCl2 and 0.5 mM MgCl2 to preserve OMV membrane integrity as previously described. OMVs were quantified by light scattering and UV absorbance, as described.
Cryo-EM.

Purified OMVs (3 muL of ~1 mg/mL) were applied to a glow-discharged Quantifoil 300-mesh gold grid in a Vitrobot chamber (ThermoFisher Mark IV). Excess liquid was blotted with a blot force of 3, blot time of 6 s, and the grid was plunge-frozen into liquid ethane. Imaging was performed on a ThermoFisher Glacios 200 kV electron microscope equipped with a Falcon 4 direct electron detector, and Selectris energy filter. Micrographs were collected with a magnification of 100 kx, a pixel size of 1.089 A/pixel, and a total dose of 60 e-/A2. Images were processed using Cryosparc v4.4.
Negative Stain EM.

Samples were adsorbed onto glow-discharged 400 mesh Formvar carbon copper grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences, PA) for 15 s, and then wicked away with filter paper. The grids were then treated with 2% uranyl-acetate for 30 s, then blotted to remove the stain, and allowed to dry for at least 1 h prior imaging at 100,000x magnification on a Jeol JEM-1400 Transmission Electron Microscope (JEOL USA, MA) at 60 kV. For each experiment, 500 OMVs were selected for measurement using FIJI.
Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy.

OMV samples were centrifuged into 3.2 mm zirconium rotors for solid-state NMR. Solid-state NMR experiments were performed on a 700 MHz AVANCE NEO Bruker spectrometer, equipped with a 3.2 mm E-free 1H/13C/15N probe. All experiments were acquired at a sample temperature of 4  C, with a MAS rate of 12.5 kHz, and a recycle delay of 2 s. The 90  pulse lengths for 1H, 13C, and 15N were set to 3 micros, 6 micros, and 6 micros. Heteronuclear decoupling was achieved using the spinal-64 pulse sequence with 70 kHz radiofrequency amplitude. During 1H-13C and 1H-15N CP, 30 kHz radiofrequency amplitude was used on 13C or 15N channels. The Hartmann-Hahn matching condition was set by ramping the 1H radiofrequency amplitude to maximize signal intensity. During double 1H-15N-13C CP, NCA polarization transfer was obtained with 22 kHz and 32 kHz radiofrequency spinlocks on the 13C and 15N channels, with 70 kHz continuous-wave decoupling on the 1H channel. For the TEDOR experiments, Hadamard encoding was applied with 2 ms selective I-BURP pulses on the 15N channel. NMR experimental details are provided in SI Appendix, Table S1.
Pellicle Formation.

Pellicle formation was assayed as described with minor modifications. Cells from an overnight induction were harvested by centrifugation, washed with sterile ice-cold phosphate buffer saline (PBS), and resuspended in 2 mL of M9 minimal media to OD600 = 0.5 in 15 x 100 mm glass tubes and incubated at 37  C with gentle agitation for 16 h.

After removing the cell suspensions by aspiration, the interior glass walls were treated with 2.5 mL of 100% ice-cold methanol for 5 min, air-dried overnight, and then washed three times with PBS prior to staining with 0.1% crystal violet for 10 min. The tubes were treated with 2.5 mL of crystal violet solution (0.1%) for 10 min, then rinsed twice with PBS to remove excess dye, and air dried overnight prior to imaging. Pellicle formation was determined qualitatively as a violet-stained ring at the air-liquid interface.
